chapters.title: Prologue
chapters.content:
The moon shone bright as frost, the breeze flowed cool as water, and the scenery was boundless in its clarity — the finest hour for pledging one's life beneath the flowers, for tying two hearts together beneath the pines.

And yet, there are always those who must spoil the mood.

Outside the ancient, serene palace halls, two dark figures flew in from north and south — vaulting over high walls, skimming across the lake, leaping over ornamental rockeries, threading through the covered corridors, drifting past the flower beds — and plunged straight into the depths of the palace.

One moved as if treading across still water on floating reeds, as steady as walking on flat ground.

The other was as light as a petal carried off by a passing breeze.

One was graceful and elegant.

The other was free and easy, like ink brushed without constraint.

Both moved without the faintest sound, swift as lightning — a testament to the extraordinary refinement of their qinggong.

The two dark figures came to a stop before a certain building at nearly the same moment, though each had approached from opposite sides and so neither was aware that someone else shared their purpose on this dark night. The moment they landed, both held their breath and circulated their inner energy to probe the surroundings, and each was rather pleased to discover they had not disturbed a soul. It seemed this renowned Shouling Palace was nothing so remarkable after all.

Each quietly pushed open a window, and with a swift contraction of the body — nimble as a cat — slipped inside. The windows closed silently the instant their feet touched the floor. The moment their toes met the ground, a wave of cold swept up from below, making both of them shudder at once. They wondered privately: was the flooring made of ice? How could it be so cold?

The interior of the building was very dark, save for a faint, soft glow at its center. Everything else lay in shadow. Both figures moved soundlessly toward that single point of light, stopping in unison about ten feet away, staring in silent wonder at what lay at its heart.

That glow was the light of a pearl. Suspended from the ceiling was a lotus-shaped glass palace lantern, inside which sat a pigeon-egg-sized night-luminescence pearl draped in a layer of white gauze. The gauze muted its dazzling radiance, letting only a gentle ring of soft light spill out to illuminate an area of roughly nine square feet. Beneath the lantern stood a white jade pillar, about four feet tall, its flat top supporting a flawless piece of jade one foot square, deep green and utterly pure. But more breathtaking still was what the jade cradled: two flowers.

They were blossoms of black and white, growing from a single stem, their petals fully open, each as large as a bowl. The petals curved like crescent moons — black as ink, white as snow — the white flower with dark stamens, the black flower with snow-white stamens, pressed close together, radiating a crystalline luminescence like that of fine jade, beautiful beyond reason, like something conjured from a dream.

So this was the "Lanyin Biyue" — the Orchid Fate and Jade Moon?

The rarest, most beautiful flower in the world.

For a moment, both figures were wholly enchanted by the strange bloom, marveling inwardly that such a thing could exist in this world, and each grew even more resolved to claim it. As they deliberated, their bodies moved of their own accord, hands reaching unbidden toward the flowers on the jade platform — and in that same instant, each noticed a hand reaching out from the darkness on the opposite side, aimed at the very same target. Both gave a start. In a flash of lightning, each sent a palm strike toward the shadowy figure across the way while keeping the other hand extended toward the jade platform.

Naturally, neither palm connected — both were neatly evaded — and neither managed to grasp the Lanyin Biyue. The two figures stepped past each other and stopped, both now caught in the dim glow of the pearl, each studying the other across the jade platform. Both were wrapped head to toe in black, faces hidden, features invisible — yet each could see the other's eyes, brighter than the luminescent pearl itself, gleaming in the dark like cold stars, radiating a strange and arresting light.

With perfect synchrony, the two let out a soft, disdainful grunt, then launched into motion, trading swift, precise strikes — all controlled force, all refined grappling techniques. Their opponent, however, proved equally skilled. After the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, neither had gained the upper hand. Neither dared to unleash their full power, for fear of destroying the exquisite Lanyin Biyue on the jade platform, and both feared that too much noise would draw the attention of Shouling Palace's guardians.

Again in unison, both withdrew. Though their breathing remained steady, each was privately shaken by the other's skill. They looked at the Lanyin Biyue, then at each other, brows furrowed. Both wanted the flower, but there was only one. A victor had to be determined — yet a true all-out fight would surely alert the palace. There would be no clean way out of that.

"Sigh."

Just as the two stood at an impasse, a sigh broke the silence, jolting both hearts at once. There was a third person in this building? And yet neither of them had sensed it. A wave of shame and anger rose in each — shame at having been so confident in their supreme martial arts, and fury that the other person had divided their attention.

"Two little ones, you may fight here for a hundred years if you like — but remember one thing: do not, under any circumstances, touch the Lanyin Biyue." A voice that carried a certain weathered depth drifted softly through the air.

Both figures looked in the direction of the voice but saw no one. They could not tell where the speaker was concealed, which only deepened their alarm and indignation.

Alarmed by the person's unfathomable depth, and angered by the contempt in his tone.

Hmph! You tell me not to touch it, so I simply won't?

"If you refuse to behave, do not blame me for activating the palace's protective mechanisms." The voice seemed to read their thoughts.

The two glanced at each other, then gave a slight nod — a silent accord: first deal with this guardian, then seize the Lanyin Biyue.

At the very moment they reached this agreement, the unhurried voice spoke again: "Young ones simply don't know the height of heaven or the depth of earth. Ah." With that sigh, two light, drifting gusts of wind swept toward them.

Both channeled their inner energy and struck out with their palms, intending to meet the force head-on — but the gentle breeze that reached them carried the weight of a thousand pounds. Both snapped to alertness instantly, drawing on every technique they had ever learned: withdrawing their hands, twisting at the waist, spinning the body, diving sideways. Using every last ounce of their power, they finally broke free of the wind that had enveloped them. When they raised their heads, they found themselves each standing beneath the window through which they had entered, far from the Lanyin Biyue.

In that moment, both were no longer merely alarmed — they were afraid. The person hidden in the darkness was still nowhere to be seen, yet every thought and movement of theirs had been entirely within his grasp. They understood clearly now: they were no match for him. There would be no taking the Lanyin Biyue tonight.

Their minds turned swiftly, their decisions were made in an instant. A hand reached out, a toe pushed off the floor, and the windows were thrown open as both slipped out, racing back the way they had come, down the mountain and out of the palace grounds.

"These two young ones are rather fine," the weathered voice within mused aloud. "I wonder which of them will one day claim the Lanyin Biyue?"

Once outside Shouling Palace, the two had begun to descend the mountain in opposite directions — one to the south, one to the north. But partway down each changed course, and after a short while, both spotted the other's figure flying toward them through the night.

They stopped. They looked at each other.

This person, if not eliminated, will surely be a formidable enemy in the days ahead.

In that moment, each harbored the exact same thought.

"Greetings, fellow traveler." Both cupped their hands and bowed at precisely the same time.

"I have always thought highly of my own martial abilities, yet tonight I find myself humbled by you. I would very much like to make your acquaintance — I only hope you will not think me unworthy." The voice from the south was clear and bright, unmistakably that of a youth not yet come of age.

"I have always delighted in befriending heroes and men of talent. Your skill is exceptional — you are precisely the kind of friend I have longed for." The voice from the north was equally clear, though with a slight roughness — the very mark of a young man still growing.

From this it could be inferred that the one from the north was perhaps slightly older, though both had lean, tall frames of nearly the same height — so the difference could not have been great.

"Wonderful! To have you as a friend — I am the most fortunate man alive." The southerner walked happily toward the northerner.

"It is my honor to have met you." The northerner walked just as happily toward the southerner.

They quickened their steps, drew close, and simultaneously stretched out their hands to clasp each other's, gripping tightly and shaking with something like excitement — the very picture of two kindred spirits meeting by chance after a lifetime apart. That is, of course, if they could have removed the black veils that still covered their faces.

"This Ying Mountain gathers the souls of heroes. To have met you here tonight, I truly wish we could drink and sing together. But I have pressing matters that prevent me from lingering. Let us make a pact: same place, same time, tomorrow night." The southerner slowly released the other's hand.

The northerner also gradually let go. "What a coincidence — I too have a prior engagement. Then let us be agreed: tomorrow night, same time, same place, and we shall drink together like brothers. I will not leave unless you come."

"Then farewell for now." The southerner clasped his hands.

"Farewell." The northerner did the same.

If you are still alive tomorrow, there will be time enough to kill you then. Each thought privately.

With that, both turned and departed, moving with such speed they might have been arrows loosed from a bow. In moments, both had reached the foot of the mountain.

"Pfft." The southerner spat a mouthful of fresh red blood and crumpled against the base of a tree.

"Thud." The northerner collapsed into the undergrowth, blood — black blood — seeping from his eyes, nostrils, the corners of his mouth, and his ears.

This was the thirty-ninth year of the Yinghua reign of the Imperial Dynasty. The dynasty had stood for one hundred and sixty-two years since its founding, through the rule of eight emperors — a time of unprecedented prosperity and splendor.

Yet the martial world was far from peaceful.

It was common knowledge that the Imperial Dynasty had, one hundred and sixty-two years ago, been a vassal state of the Eastern Dynasty. As the Eastern Dynasty crumbled and wars erupted across the land, men of ambition drew their swords and rose up in pursuit of unrivaled glory. Among those figures who shaped that turbulent era, three stood out as the most powerful and most widely supported: Huangchao of the Imperial Kingdom, Feng Lanxi of the Feng Kingdom, and Feng Xiyun of the Wind Kingdom. The Imperial King Huangchao wed Princess Hua Chunran of the Hua Kingdom, forging an alliance between the two states and greatly expanding his power, while King Feng Lanxi of the Feng Kingdom and the Wind Queen Feng Xiyun joined their nations in wedlock and combined forces to contest the realm against the Imperial King. Just as both sides had each claimed half the known world and were poised for a final, decisive battle at Dongdan, the two kings of Wind and Feng issued a proclamation — citing their unwillingness to see the common people suffer further from the ravages of war — abdicated their thrones, entrusted their kingdoms to the Imperial King, and together withdrew from the world. Thus the Imperial King unified the realm and ascended to the dragon throne, becoming the founding emperor of the Imperial Dynasty, the Emperor Chaoxi.

Who could have foreseen that though the realm was pacified, the martial world remained mired in chaos and unending conflict? The two recluses, Wind and Feng, again stepped forward, and at the foot of Ying Mountain they used the "Lanyin Order" to subdue the assembled heroes of all sects, and with the "Biyue Flower" brought together the bold spirits of the underworld, unifying the martial world and commanding its heroes. Only then did the land truly emerge from the age of slaughter and attain genuine peace. As a result, whether common folk or martial heroes, all revered and submitted to them from the bottom of their hearts. Because both had once been kings, and now stood as the lords of the martial world, combined with the names they had earned in their youth wandering the jianghu — "White Wind Dusk" and "Black Feng Xi" (together known as "White Wind Black Feng") — the martial world conferred upon them the honorific of "Wind Sovereign, Feng Emperor."

Yet for all their breathtaking brilliance, both were creatures of impulse who acted as their hearts directed and lived as they pleased. They held the throne of the martial world for no more than ten years before both abdicated and vanished once more. The assembled heroes of the martial world lamented the loss of these two unrivaled lords — yet after lamenting, more than a few quietly felt relieved. Who, after all, could resist being moved by the position of martial world sovereign? And so the heroes gathered again at Ying Mountain to select a new overlord to command the jianghu. But all were disappointed. "White Wind Dusk's" sworn younger brother, Han Pu, overwhelmed the assembled champions through sheer force of skill, seized the Lanyin Biyue, and ascended to the throne of the martial world.

He — demanded that all address him as the "Martial Emperor."

He was also the only ruler in the history of the martial world to have held sway over both the orthodox and the unorthodox paths simultaneously.

The martial world had long been divided into the White Path and the Black Path. When the "White Wind and Black Feng" ruled over the martial world, the two were husband and wife, one body, and both paths rested equally in their hands, each path honoring them as its sovereign. Yet even as the two ruled both paths, they understood that the two could never truly be merged into one, and so they used the "Lanyin Order" to command the White Path and the "Biyue Flower" to command the Black Path — and thus the martial world entered a period of balance and relative calm.

"Martial Emperor" Han Pu, through his supreme martial skill, his brilliance, and the force of his character, won the admiration and submission of every hero under heaven. He ruled the martial world for twenty years. Combined with the ten years of White Wind and Black Feng, that was the most tranquil thirty-year span the martial world had ever known. In his twilight years, Han Pu abdicated and retired to Fog Mountain, and the position of martial world overlord stood vacant once more. But the martial world did not descend into chaos over the succession. After all, decades of rule under "White Wind, Black Feng" and the Martial Emperor had transformed the jianghu — it was no longer the place where one killed at a glance of displeasure or seized treasure at the first twitch of desire. All manner of codes and regulations had long since taken root, and when Han Pu departed, he left behind the Shouling Palace.

The mountain once called "Fallen Petals Mountain," which had swallowed countless heroes during the chaos of the Eastern Dynasty's collapse, was renamed "Ying Mountain" — Mountain of Heroes — after the Wind King annihilated seventy thousand Eastern Dynasty imperial troops there.

In the early years of the Imperial Dynasty, when "White Wind and Black Feng" had gathered the martial world's heroes there to be commanded, Ying Mountain became sacred ground in the hearts of all martial people — a place where heroic souls converged. During their reign, they had built palaces on Ying Mountain to serve as their residence, and Han Pu had lived there as well. Thus Ying Mountain also came to symbolize the dwelling place of the martial world's supreme ruler.

Shouling Palace stood at the very summit of Ying Mountain. The Lanyin Biyue was kept within its halls, and its guardians — the Shouling people — were personally chosen and trained by Han Pu, passed down from generation to generation. The palace was filled with countless mechanisms and traps. Before his departure, Han Pu had issued one final decree: until a new sovereign arises, guard the Order within the palace. Those who presume to touch or seize it shall be killed without mercy.

Until a new master of the martial world was chosen, the Lanyin Biyue would remain under the protection of Shouling Palace, and no sect was permitted to make any unauthorized move. Only when a new sovereign arose would the palace present it to them. There had been those who refused to believe and harbored covert ambitions — but all of them had gone in and never come back, either dying beneath a guardian's sword or perishing in the mechanisms. After that, the myriad people of the martial world truly restrained themselves and dared not act rashly. They gathered at Ying Mountain for the Grand Assembly and competed openly for the position of martial world sovereign.

Yet the martial world of this era, after thirty years of recuperation and growth, had seen every sect and clan sink deep roots, grow steadily in strength, and cultivate new talent in abundance — a matter for rejoicing, yet also one in which the seeds of disaster had quietly taken hold. Those who are strong invariably resist having others stand over their heads, and equally dislike having to share power with anyone else. Thus, all harbored the ambition to stand alone as the ruler of the martial world. Moreover, as time accumulated, the contradictions between factions and the grudges between sects grew ever deeper and more numerous, skirmishes and killings became more frequent and commonplace, and beneath the martial world's placid surface, ambition stirred restlessly.

In the thirty-ninth year of Yinghua, the "Lanyin Order Master" Bai Zhao passed away, and the "Biyue Honor Master" Zhan Yu simultaneously abdicated. The Lanyin Biyue was returned to Shouling Palace, and the master of the martial world was to be decided anew.

In the thirty-ninth year of Yinghua, two people secretly infiltrated Shouling Palace on Ying Mountain — and left without succeeding.

These two figures, who would one day shake the entire martial world to its core, were at this moment still youths who had not yet come of age. Ying Mountain was the site of their first encounter. That night, neither knew who the other was — they only sensed it: that the other was strong, and would one day be a formidable rival.

That year should have been the time for both to make their grand debut in the jianghu, dazzling the world with their brilliance. But that friendly handshake at the foot of Ying Mountain delayed each other's ascent to the summit of the martial world.

For one had sustained a shock to the heart's meridians, and the other had been poisoned to the five viscera.

They each returned home to recover and purge the toxin, and in doing so spent five full years, missing the Lanyin Biyue of the thirty-ninth year of Yinghua entirely.

When they met again, both their martial skill and their minds had reached their absolute peak — unrivaled in all the martial world.

When they met again, each was the other's most formidable opponent. Each was the other's most important enemy.

That year was the thirty-ninth year of Yinghua. The new "Lanyin Order Master" was Ming Kong, and the "Biyue Honor Master" was Sui Qinghan.

chapters.title: Chapter One: A First Meeting Amid River Mist and Splendid Hues (Part One)
chapters.content:
At dusk, the setting sun sprinkled a light crimson veil across the western sky, draping heaven and earth, rivers and mountains, grass and trees alike in a radiant, glowing brilliance. Drifting clouds cast graceful shadows on the river's surface, and a gentle breeze off the water swayed with the reeds and rushes, dancing in time with the evening's melody. The rippling light of the river breathed out a magnificent, alluring beauty.

A white sail cut lightly through that gossamer veil, gliding as freely as a white feather drifting between heaven and earth, then darting forward swift as a white arrow over the river's surface.

On the riverbank, someone hurrying along happened to glance up and found themselves bewitched by the splendor of the evening clouds and the river scene. They stopped, gaze drawn toward that white sail. Gradually it drew closer. At the bow of the boat stood a figure clothed in pale green, vivid against the crimson evening glow yet in perfect harmony with it — as though all the gorgeous color filling the sky and earth and water had been brought into being for this one person alone. Like a stalk of jade-green bamboo rising tall and clear through the rose-tinted mist, the figure added a quality of pure, transcendent beauty to the already splendid scene, bringing the painted dusk to life in an instant. The person watching from the bank felt as though they had returned, at last, to the world of the living.

As the light boat passed before them, the person on the bank found themselves smiling instinctively at the pale-green figure standing at the bow. The distance between them was great, the other's form indistinct, their face impossible to make out — and yet the watcher felt certain that the figure had smiled back. In that moment, their heart filled with a quiet joy, the weariness of the road vanishing without a trace. Their gaze followed that figure, followed the swift-fading silhouette of the boat, until the sky and earth grew dark.

In the dim and fading light, the watcher came back to themselves. Looking out over the empty river, a faint regret stirred within — regret for not having called out a greeting to the one on the boat, regret for not having found a way to meet them. How good it would have been to have known that person — they would have been the first friend he had made since entering the jianghu.

If only they had met that once, perhaps things would have unfolded quite differently.

Many years later, he would always think of it that way.

That was — the first time Ning Lang ever saw Lan Canyin, in the midst of a sky, an earth, and a river all ablaze with gorgeous evening light, as though it were not quite of this world.

It was also the first time Ning Lang had set foot in the jianghu. He was nineteen years old that year.

He had gone up Qianbei Mountain to study at the age of four, and for a full fifteen years had not come down until this past third month. Though his parents had visited him every year on the mountain, it had still been more than ten years since he had been home. All those years, what he had longed for day and night was the great tree behind the house and the wooden sword hidden in the secret cave — so when he finally came down, he had intended to stay by his parents' side and care for them well, to enjoy the warmth of family at last. But not even a full month had passed before his mother sent him on an urgent errand to the Lan family in Yun Province.

The thought of that urgent errand made Ning Lang's slightly dark face flush a little, his heart beating just a touch faster. And yet — when he had arrived at the Lan family estate, dusty from travel, half excited and half anxious, the steward had told him that the master of the house had gone out and that the date of return was uncertain. He felt at once disappointed and, in some inexplicable way, relieved.

Once out of the Lan estate, he thought: since he was already out, there was no great rush to go home. His parents were in fine health, so there was nothing to worry about. He might as well wander the jianghu for a while. His mother always said that a man ought to build something of his own, and his older fellow disciples had always lit up when speaking of the jianghu. He would go and see it for himself.

And in looking, he was drawn into a whirl of gorgeous color, and out of it stepped a legend that would shake the world.

Many years later, looking back in a moment of sudden clarity and remembering the feelings of this moment, all he could do was let out a long, quiet sigh.

If he could do it again — would he still want to look?

The him of this moment would say yes.

The him of many years later could only smile faintly and leave it unanswered.

The fifth month. Yuzhou, in the city of Yu.

On a street to the west of the city, neither particularly bustling nor especially quiet, there stood a residence neither particularly grand nor in any way poor. The large lacquered doors were banded with brass, and while there were no stone lions or tigers standing guard at the entrance to project an air of authority, two burly servants kept watch.

The wide courtyard, spanning several mu of land, held no carved railings or ornate stonework. A few winding covered walkways curved like ribbons through the grounds, and several pavilions and small buildings stood among the flowering trees, spaced with easy openness. Climbing roses covered the lattice frames in thick clusters that from a distance looked like pink clouds, and a pomegranate tree blazed in full scarlet bloom at the center of the yard. In the very heart of the courtyard was a round pond of several zhang across, its surface scattered with broad lotus leaves and a few budding stems. A small pavilion stood alone in the middle of the water, bamboo curtains hanging on all four sides, swaying in the pleasant breeze.

"...That is the latest news from Yun Province." A middle-aged man with a pale face and a sparse white beard stood beside the pond, reporting to someone inside the water pavilion. "And the matter here in Yu City has been settled as per your instructions."

Within the bamboo curtains, a hazy green silhouette was faintly visible.

"Does the Seventh Young Master have any other instructions?" The middle-aged man raised his head slightly to ask.

His words had barely fallen when a faint clamor drifted in from outside the courtyard — followed shortly by the sound of clashing steel. The middle-aged man could not help but feel a slight unease, his gaze darting nervously toward the pavilion on the water.

The pavilion was silent for a good while before a single, unhurried reply came: "You may step aside for now." The voice was extremely soft, yet it stirred something in the chest without reason.

"Yes." The middle-aged man hastened to comply and had nearly reached the courtyard gate when it was thrown open with a loud bang, and then — two more bangs — two figures came flying in and landed hard on the ground.

Before the middle-aged man could react, a striking young man had already strode in with a confident shout: "I'm looking for your master!" In one hand he held a gleaming silver spear roughly the length of a sword; with the other, he gripped a cringing old man by the arm.

The middle-aged man stepped forward and clasped his hands. "I am Nie Chongyuan, and I happen to be the master of this house. What is your reason, sir, for forcing your way in like this?"

"You're the master here? I am Ning Lang, and it's you I'm looking for!" The young man had a face and a voice to match his name — and all the clear-cut sense of justice natural to someone his age. "Sunset Tower is that old uncle's family inheritance, passed down through generations. How dare you seize it by force — and then throw the old man out of his own home, leaving him to wander the streets! You...you...for a grown man to bully an old person like this — how can you!" Ning Lang looked at Nie Chongyuan with blazing, forthright eyes, his handsome face flushed red with anger.

Nie Chongyuan's brow furrowed. He glanced at the old man, and the moment that gaze landed on him, the scrawny old figure shrank back and cowered behind Ning Lang. Ning Lang noticed clearly, and his anger rose several degrees at once. Where there is righteousness, there must be protection of the weak and punishment of the wicked.

"Elder Yue..." Nie Chongyuan shifted his feet, trying to get a clear look at the old man.

"What do you think you're doing?!" Ning Lang shouted immediately and stepped forward to block the old man.

Nie Chongyuan stopped and looked Ning Lang over, then raised his hand to beckon a servant over and gave him a quiet instruction. The servant nodded and turned to leave.

Meanwhile, the old man tugged gently at Ning Lang's sleeve and said softly, "Young hero Ning, let us... let us go back."

"Why?" Ning Lang turned, and reading the fear on the old man's face, understood immediately. "Don't be afraid, Uncle. I will protect you. I will see justice done for you today."

"It would be better... better to let it go..." the old man said, eyes downcast, glancing toward Nie Chongyuan.

"How can we let it go!" Ning Lang refused. "They seized your livelihood and drove a solitary old man out into the streets. How can something like this be let go?! Don't be afraid of them, Uncle. While I'm here, I won't let them bully you."

"But..." the old man wavered, trying to say something.

Just then, the servant who had left came hurrying back, carrying a wooden box. Nie Chongyuan opened the lock, then gestured toward Ning Lang, signaling the servant to present it to him.

Ning Lang looked at the box now before him, then shot a slightly suspicious glance at Nie Chongyuan.

"Have a look, young hero, and you'll understand," said Nie Chongyuan, composed and unruffled.

Ning Lang opened the box. Inside was a sheaf of papers — some old, some new. He picked them up one by one and began to read. At first he was puzzled, then gradually his understanding grew, and the expression on his face changed.

Nie Chongyuan observed this quietly, and smiled slightly. "These are all the debt documents of this Elder Yue, along with the deed by which he transferred Sunset Tower to me in settlement of his debts. Everything is in black and white — please read them carefully, young hero."

"You..." Ning Lang turned to look at the old man behind him, only to find him head bowed, body hunched, a picture of misery. His heart gave a surge of warmth, and he turned back to glare at Nie Chongyuan. "Even if these are genuine, they could still have been fabricated by you. How could Elder Yue, with such a thriving establishment as Sunset Tower, have run up this much debt!"

Nie Chongyuan sighed, seeming somewhat helpless, and addressed the old man who stood there with bowed head and averted eyes: "Elder Yue, did you truly not tell young hero Ning the truth?"

"What... what truth..." the old man muttered, edging slightly backward.

"What truth?" Ning Lang looked between the old man and Nie Chongyuan.

Since Elder Yue showed no sign of speaking, Nie Chongyuan had no choice but to continue: "Elder Yue became obsessed with women and addicted to gambling, and long ago squandered every last coin of his family fortune. Beyond that, he used Sunset Tower as collateral to accumulate ninety thousand silver leaves of debt with Rain Forest Tower and Taifeng Gambling Den — and Sunset Tower alone falls far short of repaying what is owed." He paused, seeing Ning Lang's brow tighten, clearly able to guess what the young man was thinking. He continued: "You may not believe my word alone, young hero, or you may feel I arranged all of this. So you are welcome to go and ask around the city — there are many in this town who were once close to Elder Yue and have since distanced themselves because of his gambling and his vices. Or better yet, you can ask Elder Yue himself."

Hearing this, Ning Lang turned to the old man: "Uncle, is what he said true?"

"He... he..." The old man's scrawny face turned red, but he could not manage to put a complete sentence together.

Nie Chongyuan, watching him, let an expression of profound regret settle over his face. "The courtesan Yun Wu of Rain Forest Tower is famed throughout Yuzhou for her beauty, but everyone in this city knows her price — a thousand taels for a single night. Only a man of considerable fortune could afford to keep her company. Yet Elder Yue spent night after night in Yun Wu's chambers, and even a fortune of a million can be emptied in time. And while 'Taifeng Gambling Den' is among my own establishments, I myself urged Elder Yue on many occasions to stop — but not only did he refuse, he bet ever larger sums, running up mountains of gambling debt. Sunset Tower, left unattended and mismanaged, was on the verge of closing down. Left with no other choice, I purchased Sunset Tower to cut off the temptation, and settled his debts at Rain Forest Tower on his behalf. I also gave him two hundred silver leaves — enough, if spent carefully, to buy a small house, start a small business, and live out his remaining years in comfort. Who would have thought he spent it all in a single day and then..." Nie Chongyuan trailed off with a deep, heavy sigh, looking at Elder Yue with an expression of anguish and helplessness.

At this, Elder Yue's already red face deepened further in color, and his frail, bony frame began to tremble ever so slightly.

Ning Lang, having heard it all, took one look at Elder Yue's expression and understood at once — a wave of shock and fury washing over him in equal measure.

At noon that very day, he had just entered Yuzhou. He had heard his older fellow disciples on Qianbei Mountain speak of Sunset Tower's fame and had intended to try the legendary Broken Swan wine for himself. But at the entrance to Sunset Tower, he had found an old man sitting on the ground in the blazing midday sun, muttering to himself with an expression of despairing anguish. He had felt a pang of compassion and gone over to inquire. The moment the old man noticed him approaching, he grabbed hold of him and burst into tears, going on about the bitterness of having his livelihood seized, the hardship of drifting homeless in the streets, and the sorrow of having been abandoned by everyone he knew. Ning Lang, barely a day into the jianghu and brimming with righteous fire, had listened and felt his temper blaze immediately. He grabbed the old man and marched him to Nie Manor to demand justice. At the gate, the two door guards had refused to let them in, claiming the master was resting and must not be disturbed. The arrogant way they looked down at him had fanned his anger three degrees hotter, so he had struck the two servants a lesson and forced his way in — only to arrive at a truth quite like this.

"Uncle, how...how could you deceive me?" Ning Lang stared at Elder Yue with wide, round eyes.

"I...I only wanted someone to hear my grievances," Elder Yue defended himself, hearing Ning Lang's accusation. "I had no idea you would take it so seriously and drag me all the way here. I...I never asked you to come..." That last line was clearly spoken with a guilty conscience, the voice barely audible.

"But you had no right to tell me lies!" Ning Lang said loudly.

Elder Yue shrank under the shout, backing up a few steps. He was afraid this young hero who had split open Nie Manor's gate with a single palm might do the same to him. "Why are you shouting like that?" he said.

"This is merely a misunderstanding resolved." From the side, Nie Chongyuan smiled gently — and in the very next breath added, "Young hero, there is no need to be upset. Only, in the future, perhaps do not be so hasty when it comes to acts of chivalry."

"I...I..." Ning Lang felt his face go scarlet — this time not from anger, but from shame.

Nie Chongyuan waved a hand magnanimously. "The young hero acted out of good intentions. I hold no grudge."

"I'm sorry — I damaged your gate, and I will pay for it. And these two gentlemen, I apologize for striking you. You may strike me back. If you're hurt, I have medicine with me — my master gave it to me. It works very well. Here, take it..." Ning Lang bowed and apologized, offered money, then dug out medicine, all in a breathless flurry, his handsome face flushed dark red beneath his tan, a sight so endearingly flustered that it was hard not to laugh.

Nie Chongyuan was a seasoned man of the jianghu and could see at once that today's incident was nothing more than the well-meaning impulsiveness of a young man new to the world — a good heart, but a touch too hasty. Furthermore, it had all happened right in front of the Seventh Young Master. Thinking this over, Nie Chongyuan felt a flicker of apprehension: what if the Seventh Young Master blamed him for handling things poorly?

While he was still mulling this over, a soft voice called from the water pavilion: "Chongyuan."

At that voice, both Ning Lang, who had been fumbling for medicine, and Elder Yue, who had been edging toward the exit, stopped short in their tracks. The voice was clear yet bewitching, soothing to the ear and softening to the bones — and impossible to place as either male or female. Ning Lang's heart lurched; his hands clenched too hard, and with a clatter, everything he had been holding tumbled to the ground. He did not dare to move.

chapters.title: Chapter One: A First Meeting Amid River Mist and Splendid Hues (Part Two)
chapters.content:
"What are your instructions, Seventh Young Master?" Nie Chongyuan turned at once to face the pavilion, his manner respectful.

Within the bamboo curtains, the green silhouette stirred — as though someone had risen and moved toward the edge of the curtain. Yet those standing in the courtyard could still not make out the figure within, only a hazy, indistinct shadow, all the more intriguing for it.

"Since it was a misunderstanding, treat Young Hero Ning as a proper guest. This Elder Yue is advanced in years — have another two hundred silver leaves sent to him to help him get by." The green silhouette within gave these instructions in an unhurried tone.

"Yes, as the Seventh Young Master commands." Nie Chongyuan bowed to receive the order, then told a servant to fetch two hundred silver leaves. He turned to Ning Lang and said, "If Young Hero Ning does not find it beneath him, please allow me to offer a little hospitality."

"No...no, thank you." Ning Lang was so mortified he would have gladly sunk into a hole in the ground, and had no thought of staying as a guest. "I'm...I'm sorry. I'll be going now. If there's anything you need in the future, come find me — I'll do whatever I can to help." Leaving those words behind, without bothering to pick up the things strewn across the courtyard, he turned and strode away. He glanced back once and caught Elder Yue staring fixedly at the water pavilion, which stirred a feeling of quiet distaste in him. He said nothing and left without a word.

Shortly after, the servant returned with the silver leaves, and Nie Chongyuan sent Elder Yue on his way. Quiet returned to the courtyard.

"Chongyuan, you handled this matter well." The clear, alluring voice from within the pavilion carried a faint note of amusement.

"I would not dare take the credit," Nie Chongyuan quickly replied. "It was all thanks to the Seventh Young Master's advice to 'give him what he desires' — without that, I would still have been at a complete loss."

"Ha...give him what he desires..." A light, easy laugh drifted from the pavilion. "Whatever the case, you did well this time. I will have you manage Sunset Tower as well."

"Many thanks, Seventh Young Master." Nie Chongyuan bowed in pleased gratitude.

"I truly could not have imagined that this Elder Yue, half of his body already in the grave, could still be so utterly bewitched by feminine beauty." There was still a trace of amusement in the Seventh Young Master's voice, along with a cool, faint disdain. "People in this world simply cannot escape two things: wealth and desire." With these words, the green silhouette within the pavilion shifted, and the figure seemed to lie back down.

Nie Chongyuan hesitated a moment, then said, "This matter went so smoothly — Yun Wu deserves no small share of the credit."

"Oh?" came the Seventh Young Master's idle reply, followed by a casual inquiry: "How has Yun Wu been lately?"

"The young lady is in fine health. She misses the Seventh Young Master deeply." Nie Chongyuan steeled himself to say it, thinking: Yun Wu, you did me a great favor, and now I'll risk a word on your behalf in return. Whether it comes to anything depends entirely on how much weight the Seventh Young Master places on you.

"Is that so." The Seventh Young Master's reply was light and flat — neither pleased nor displeased. But after a pause came a remark that left Nie Chongyuan pleasantly surprised: "There is nothing particularly interesting here in Yuzhou. I suppose I may as well go and see her."

"Then I will have someone sent ahead to inform her." Nie Chongyuan immediately followed up.

"No need." The silhouette within the pavilion stirred slightly — a hand seemed to wave dismissively. "I will go when I choose. You attend to your own affairs."

"Yes." Nie Chongyuan bowed his head and was about to turn and leave when the Seventh Young Master called him back.

"That Ning Lang today — what do you make of him?"

Nie Chongyuan considered for a moment before replying: "He appears to be a young disciple newly out from some sect, making his first venture into the jianghu. Judging by his bearing and physique, his martial foundation is extremely solid — with time and experience in the jianghu, he will certainly become a figure of consequence. For now, however, he is nothing more than a headstrong young calf, and not yet worth concerning oneself over."

"Hmm." The Seventh Young Master seemed to agree. "Did you notice the spear he was carrying?"

"A silver spear? Surely not...he is from the Ning family?" Nie Chongyuan said with some surprise.

"Indeed. He should be from the Ning family of Lan Province." There was an inexplicable note of quiet amusement in that clear, beguiling voice. "When your people encounter him in the future, remember to treat him with courtesy. And in conducting your business — be mindful of avoiding him."

"Understood." Nie Chongyuan complied. Though inwardly he was somewhat puzzled — while the Ning family of Lan Province was certainly one of the six great clans of the martial world, the Seventh Young Master was not in the habit of avoiding trouble. Why, then, this unusual caution toward a Ning Lang who posed no threat whatsoever?

"That will be all. You may go."

"Yes." And this time, Nie Chongyuan truly withdrew.

When the courtyard was completely empty, the bamboo curtain was lifted aside, and a green-clad figure stepped out. In that instant, the plain, refined courtyard seemed to suddenly don a garment of splendor — the roses and pomegranate blooms turned gaudy with shame.

That person glanced at the heap of things Ning Lang had left by the pond, and a faint smile lifted the corner of their lips. "Ning Lang...what a delightfully amusing person. But after years in this jianghu — will he still be the same?"

The soft laughter faded gently away, leaving behind an inexplicable, lingering longing.

At dusk.

On a street in Yuzhou, a young man in blue wandered along with a troubled expression, his gaze drifting now and then toward the entrance of a restaurant — swallowing once before pulling his eyes away and continuing slowly down the road.

This young man was none other than Ning Lang. In his frantic dash from Nie Manor, he had forgotten to retrieve his belongings from the courtyard, and now found himself completely without funds. At noon, having believed every word Elder Yue told him, he had charged off to Nie Manor in a righteous fury and completely forgotten to eat. And now it was dinnertime. Passersby hurried homeward along the street, and every inn and restaurant wafted out thick, mouthwatering aromas that made the empty siege inside his stomach even more dramatic — yet he truly had no face to go back to Nie Manor and ask for his silver leaves.

What to do? What to do? No money meant no food, no place to sleep, and certainly no future in the jianghu. And it would be difficult to simply go home from here — there was no one he knew in this city to borrow from. What on earth was he to do?

Ning Lang walked on, beset by these worries.

"Yun Wu, Yun Wu — I have come to see you."

A voice, faintly familiar — clear and beguiling — drifted into his ears. Ning Lang followed it instinctively, and there, ten paces ahead, stood a building. Its sign bore three large characters in rosy red: Rain Forest Tower.

"Yun Wu, Yun Wu — I have come to see you."

The voice sounded again, brushing lightly against the heart, and Ning Lang walked toward it without thinking.

He entered to find a wide, opulent hall filled with gold and jade. Standing in the center of the room, back toward him, was a pale yellow figure — upright and graceful, an image that "jade tree in the wind" fell far short of capturing. Everyone in the hall — whether singing, playing instruments, or chatting and laughing, men and women alike — turned their heads at once, faces going still with wonder and enchantment. And upstairs, doors flew open one after another with rapid bangs, and a parade of slender figures in reds, greens, blues, and purples poured out — some with hair still unbound, some with robes half open, some without shoes — the cries from behind them entirely ignored.

"It's the Seventh Young Master! It's the Seventh Young Master!"

"Seventh Young Master, I finally get to see you again!"

"Seventh Young Master, you've come at last!"

"Seventh Young Master...Seventh Young Master..."

The hall rang with a chorus of melodious voices, a flutter of red sleeves from every direction — yet the figure in pale yellow only tilted his head slightly, and with one single sweeping glance, the entire hall fell into silence, followed by a ripple of sighs.

It was at that moment that a voice, beautiful as the music of celestial maidens, rang out: "Seventh Young Master..."

Soft and lingering, laden with boundless feeling. Before the sound had even faded, a figure in jade-green vaulted lightly from the carved railing overhead, plunging downward like a swallow that had lost its wings.

"Ah!" A collective cry of alarm rose from the entire building, and some of the more timid souls squeezed their eyes shut.

"Yun Wu." That quiet utterance carried the quality of a lover's drowsy murmur in the deep of night — unguarded, and therefore most sincere. Who could remain untouched? The pale yellow figure rose lightly into the air, one arm extending mid-flight to encircle the jade-clad beauty's slender waist. Robes billowing, the two descended like immortals alighting from the heavens.

"Ah!" This time the entire hall erupted in a collective sigh of longing. "Seventh Young Master! Seventh Young Master! I want that too!" Every beauty in the building wished with all her heart that she were the one caught in the Seventh Young Master's arms.

A single slender finger rose and gently wagged once — and all the clamor died instantly.

"Seventh Young Master, you've finally come to see Yun Wu." The beauty of peerless complexion tilted her face upward, gazing with rapt devotion at the figure before her, lost in the depths of those eyes shimmering like still water lit by moonlight.

The Seventh Young Master broke into a smile, warm and beguiling. "I have come to see you."

"You've finally come." Yun Wu closed her eyes and nestled against his shoulder, wishing this single moment could stretch into eternity.

Envy and longing rippled through the hall.

"It has been a long time since I heard Yun Wu play the xiao," the Seventh Young Master said softly, one hand gently patting her. "I do miss it."

Yun Wu raised her head at these words and said quietly: "Every night, the jade xiao plays — waiting only for you."

The Seventh Young Master extended his right hand, and a white jade fan unfurled like the moon opening. He said slowly: "The xiao drifts pale, the player fair as jade — why speak of not trading the mortal world for the moon above. Play a melody for me, Yun Wu."

"Gladly." Yun Wu led him toward the stairs.

At the foot of the staircase, the Seventh Young Master suddenly turned back, his gaze drifting to settle on the doorway from afar.

In that instant, Ning Lang heard a sound — a great "thud." Only much later did he realize it had been the sound of his own heartbeat.

The Seventh Young Master's jade fan swayed lightly, half-concealing a smile. Those eyes swept briefly to the side — and then the figure turned and ascended the stairs.

Perhaps it was the great distance, or perhaps that glance had been too brief — Ning Lang had not caught the face clearly. Yet those eyes had already sent his mind reeling.

They say the water of Heaven Lake at the summit of Jiulun Mountain is the clearest, purest water in the world — formed from snowmelt fallen from the nine heavens above.

They say the cold jade of Kunwu's Canglei Abyss is the greenest, most flawless jade in the world — shaped by the essence of spirit gathered at the bottom of the nine abysses.

Those eyes were like Kunwu's jade sunk in the waters of Jiulun's heavenly lake.

And yet — it was not only that.

In childhood, on summer nights when the family sat outside in the cool air, his mother would fan him with a bamboo fan and tell him stories. The stories were full of fox spirits and demons and monsters lurking in deep mountains and ancient forests — creatures that needed only one glance at a mortal to snatch away their very soul, leaving them either mad or dead.

Those undulating jade-green eyes possessed a soul entirely their own. And moreover... it was the soul of something not quite human.

Still new to the jianghu, Ning Lang was unfamiliar with nearly everything around him, and so he did not yet know that a pair of eyes like those were unique in all the world. Nor could he connect them with the name that resounded throughout the jianghu.

"Young Hero Ning! Young Hero Ning!"

Jolted by the sudden call, Ning Lang startled awake as if from a dream, only to realize he had been holding his breath — his chest ached with it.

"Young Hero Ning, the Seventh Young Master asked me to give this to you." A pretty young maidservant held out a bundle wrapped in brocade.

"For me?" Ning Lang accepted it in surprise and opened it — and immediately froze. Were these not the things he had dropped in Nie Manor's courtyard? His money pouch and medicine vials were all there, not a single item missing. But there was also something new — a small brocade pouch. He opened it to find several gold leaves inside. He counted: not one more, not one less — exactly seven. And on each leaf's tip, something small and fine seemed to be engraved.

"Young Hero Ning, have you counted everything? Nothing is missing?" The maidservant's eyes were fixed on his face with great care, as though she found him most curious.

"This isn't mine," Ning Lang said honestly, holding out the seven gold leaves along with the pouch toward the maidservant.

"Oh, that is the Seventh Young Master's gift to you. Please keep it." The maidservant smiled and gently pushed it back.

"The Seventh Young Master?" Ning Lang was puzzled. He did not believe he knew anyone by that name.

But the maidservant gave no explanation, saying only: "My errand is done. Please do as you like, young hero." And with that, she turned and walked away.

Ning Lang was left standing at the entrance, hand in the air, holding the gold leaves. After a long moment, he suddenly remembered the figure concealed behind bamboo curtains in Nie Manor — the one Nie Chongyuan had called "Seventh Young Master."

"Ah, so it was him." Ning Lang slowly turned away, cradling the cloth bundle, muttering in a vaguely bewildered tone: "So he is a man."

chapters.title: Chapter Two: A Son Like a Green Lotus (Part One)
chapters.content:
The sixth month, when the summer sun blazes at its most fierce.

Ning Lang had been traveling half the day and was looking around for a shady place to rest. But this was empty, open country — not even a decently sized tree anywhere, just bare rolling hills and a sun-cracked dirt road baking under the relentless heat. Just as he was resigning himself to it, a strain of qin music reached his ears, and he immediately perked up. Where there is music, there is a person, and where there is a person, there might be a household — he could go and beg a cup of water, maybe even buy some provisions. He was very hungry. With that thought, he followed the music.

The melody was faint. Worried it would stop before he found its source, Ning Lang called up his qinggong and flew forward at speed — but after a good while, still found no one. He crested another hill, and before him opened a lush, green forest with a rooftop just visible within. His spirits lifted, and he swept toward the trees.

Now closer, the music reached him clearly. The tune itself was simple, yet it carried an inexhaustible depth of feeling. And at intervals, a sharp "ding" would ring out among the strings — as though striking in harmony with the music, or perhaps trying to cut it off, a blend of two sounds at once unified and oddly discordant. Each time Ning Lang heard that "ding," a restless agitation rose in his chest, and he found himself instinctively channeling his inner energy to resist it. But the moment his inner energy stirred, his qi and blood surged in violent rebellion, his ears rang, and his vision swam. Something was very wrong — he caught himself with a start, but the internal energy was already rushing unchecked and out of control. Just as the situation turned dangerous, the music suddenly halted, and a clear, calm voice reached his ear: "Still your breath. Stop the energy."

He did so at once, and it worked — the raging qi settled, the ringing and dizziness faded, and the qin music resumed, slow and gentle.

"Do not hurt others." That calm, measured voice sounded again, softly, as though cautioning someone.

Ning Lang, now thoroughly curious, set aside all thought of hunger and thirst and pressed deeper into the forest, wanting to see who was playing.

Beyond the forest lay a bamboo grove, its tall fronds swaying lightly in the wind, their green cool and unhurried, sweeping away the stifling heat at once. The qin music continued clear and cool; the sharp "ding" still sounded at intervals, but it no longer disturbed the rhythm of his heartbeat.

He passed through the bamboo grove, and the scene before him brightened suddenly.

Ahead rose a cliff face of several zhang, draped in green moss and pale ferns, a thin stream of water trickling slowly down its face into a clear pool below, where jade-white droplets leapt up and fell back. The pool's surface was covered with broad lotus leaves and clusters of white lotus blossoms standing tall and slender. Beside the pool stood an old wooden building, elegant and simply made, connected by a floating bridge to a small pavilion half-hidden in the lotus at the center of the lake.

The sight calmed Ning Lang's mind and soothed his spirit — his hunger, thirst, and weariness vanished at once. He walked along the edge of the pool for a stretch, then stepped onto the floating bridge and made his way toward the center. From a distance, only clusters of green lotus were visible, but once inside, he could see that the lake was far wider than it looked. After nearly half a cup of tea's worth of walking, the music grew distinct. He looked up to find a small stone pavilion where two young men sat facing each other — one playing the qin, one playing a blade.

The blade player had his back to Ning Lang, dressed in black, face unseen, yet even his back radiated a quality of cold, solitary severity. He held a blade across his lap and plucked the strings with his fingers — that sharp "ding" was the sound he produced. The qin player faced him, head slightly bowed, wearing an azure robe the color of lotus leaves, with calm, refined features. His ink-black hair was half tied at the crown and half flowing to his shoulders, his whole person unadorned, clean and plain. Ringed by lotus leaves, he looked like an immortal banished to the mortal realm.

Ning Lang stopped instinctively a zhang away, not daring to intrude — but the azure-robed qin player raised his eyes and glanced at him. The man who appeared so otherworldly had a pair of eyes like mist over still water, gazing as if from across ten thousand mountains and rivers, at once immeasurably distant and deeply, movingly sincere.

"There is tea and refreshments to your side, please help yourself," said the azure-robed man with a gentle smile toward Ning Lang, seeming to know exactly how hungry and thirsty he was.

That smile alone dissolved all of Ning Lang's awe and nervousness — it felt as natural and warm as seeing an old fellow disciple. And this, he realized, was the voice that had helped him out of danger earlier. A wave of goodwill rose in him at once. He looked to the side and saw a teapot and teacups on the wide stone railing of the pavilion, along with several plates of refreshments. That was enough — the moment he saw them, his throat went dry with thirst and his hunger blazed up anew. He swallowed hard, glanced once more at the two men who were still playing, each absorbed in his own thing, and then without further ceremony walked into the pavilion, poured and drained three cups of tea to quench his thirst, and settled in to eat from the plates of refreshments. As he ate, he took a closer look at the two men.

Both were young — perhaps twenty-three or twenty-four. From his position he could now see the blade player's profile, and those features looked as though they had been cut from stone: perfect, yet sharp and severe. His eyes were closed, as if every last thing in this world were nothing more than dust. The qin player, by contrast, played with an air of casual ease — fast, then slow, then fast again. His misty eyes drifted now and then toward the blade player, then settled far away on the green lotus and white blossoms, a picture of serene, unhurried freedom.

"Shall we take a break?" The azure-robed man spoke eventually, at some point that was hard to determine.

It was framed as a question, but the hand that had been playing the qin was already still, the music gone — and the sound of the blade stopped at the exact same moment.

The blade player opened his eyes and looked at his companion. "Why is it always impossible to fight to a conclusion?"

The azure-robed man smiled gently. "You have few rivals now. There is no need to be so insistent."

"Hmph!" The black-clad blade player let out a cold, discontented sound. "You are the same as he is. But one day I will settle things clearly with both of you."

"So there is another person in this world who leaves you at a loss," the azure-robed man remarked lightly, wiping the qin strings with a silk cloth.

The black-clad man flicked his wrist and the blade snapped back into the scabbard on his back. "I find it strange myself — you and he are said to be equals in reputation, yet how have you not met each other by now?"

The azure-robed man's hand paused ever so slightly, then he lifted his head and smiled at the black-clad man. "So it is him. I have long heard his name, and have always felt it a pity that we have never crossed paths."

A faint glimmer of subtle derision passed through the blade player's eyes. "He says the same."

"If it is fated, we will meet." The azure-robed man said this without concern. He turned, and his misty eyes rested on Ning Lang. The faint smile on his face was perfectly understated. "Were the tea and refreshments to your satisfaction?" The warm timbre of his voice and the dignity of his manner made this blazing summer day feel like a gentle spring breeze.

Ning Lang's face went a little red. He stood and clasped his hands. "Thank you, sir. I...I have eaten my fill. Everything was delicious." It truly was. The tea had been cool and fragrant, and the refreshments were unlike anything he had tasted before — better than every sweet he had ever eaten. He had no idea what they were made of.

The azure-robed gentleman regarded him quietly for a moment, then smiled. "There is no need for ceremony. I am Ming Huayan — the owner of this place. And this is Lie Chifeng." He gestured toward the black-clad man, then clasped his own hands in greeting. "Just now I was idly practicing, and nearly caused you harm. My deepest apologies."

The names Ming Huayan and Lie Chifeng would have caused any person of the jianghu to stiffen at once with reverence — but as fortune would have it, the one who heard them now was Ning Lang, who had entered the jianghu barely a day ago and had managed nothing yet but one botched attempt at justice. So he simply stood there awkwardly, hands clasped, head slightly lowered, not quite daring to look directly at the gentleman who seemed as fine as a lotus bloom.

"No...not at all. I'm Ning Lang. I was passing through and heard the music and came to investigate. I've been disturbing you — I'm sorry. I'll be going now." He turned to leave, took one step, then turned back. "I'm sorry — I ate your food without paying. Let me give you something for it." He reached into his chest, pulled out his money pouch, thought for a moment, then drew a gold leaf from the brocade pouch and held it toward Ming Huayan. "Is...is this enough?" He looked up with round, inquiring eyes.

Ming Huayan was taken aback. He looked at those frank, clear eyes before him, then laughed softly. "Please put it away — those coarse trifles were an honor to share. I could not possibly accept money."

"But...that doesn't feel right. I ate your food without asking, and such good food at that." Ning Lang was genuinely troubled. He pushed the gold leaf forward a little further, and the blade player Lie Chifeng happened to glance over and catch sight of it — his eyes sharpened, and he turned to look at Ning Lang more carefully.

That one look made Ning Lang's face run cold. He felt as though those eyes were like the edge of a blade, and the man himself, simply sitting there, was like an unsheathed sword — every inch of him radiant with an edge that made one instinctively recoil. His hand trembled slightly without his willing it.

"Meeting here is itself a kind of fate. You are a man of the jianghu as well — why stand on such formalities?" Ming Huayan raised a finger and gently pushed the gold leaf aside.

"Well, this..." Ning Lang looked at the gold leaf in his hand, then at the otherworldly figure before him, and suddenly felt his gesture a kind of sacrilege. He hastily withdrew his hand — but then, thinking that made it look too obvious, as though he were reluctant to part with his own money, his face burst into flames, and the gold leaf hovered in his grip, unable to go forward or back.

Ming Huayan watched this thoroughly flustered young man with great amusement. Someone in the jianghu with a mind this simple was a rare sight indeed.

"How about this — next time, I'll treat you to a meal?" Ning Lang thought hard for a while and finally came up with a compromise, looking at Ming Huayan with bright, eager eyes.

"Agreed." Ming Huayan accepted without a moment's hesitation.

"Good, good." Ning Lang grinned, scratching his head.

"Where did you get those gold leaves?" A cold voice cut in from the side without warning.

"Huh?" Ning Lang startled and turned toward Lie Chifeng, whose gaze had settled on the gold leaf in his hand. He answered honestly: "When I was in Yuzhou, someone called the 'Seventh Young Master' gave them to me."

A sharp light flashed through Lie Chifeng's blade-like eyes. He looked Ning Lang up and down with deliberate thoroughness, then shook his head slightly — as though he found it entirely implausible that someone like this could have received a gift from the Seventh Young Master. "Who are you? Where are you from? Where are you going? What are you doing?" Four questions, asked as though they were the most natural thing in the world. Anyone else might have felt his manner was poor and his manners absent — one simply didn't interrogate a stranger like this. The only reason it worked was because Ning Lang was the one being asked.

"I'm Ning Lang. I come from Lan Province. I was going to find someone in Yun Province, but didn't find them, so now I'm just...looking around." He scratched his head with a slightly sheepish smile. "My older fellow disciples always said the jianghu was interesting..."

"Lan Province? Yun Province?" Lie Chifeng's brow moved. "Who are you looking for?"

"My mother asked me to find Lan Can...yin..." At the name, Ning Lang felt his face flush and his voice drop despite himself.

Lie Chifeng's brow gave a small, involuntary twitch. He studied Ning Lang once more, eyes settling on the silver spear across his back, then said at an unhurried pace: "In the middle of the seventh month, if you go to Longsky Manor in Hua Province, you should be able to meet them."

"Ah?" Ning Lang looked up abruptly, unable to suppress his astonishment and delight. "You mean...Lan Canyin?"

"Yes." Lie Chifeng gave a single nod.

"Who is Lan Canyin?" Ming Huayan asked from the side with mild curiosity.

Lie Chifeng looked back at him, and the faint derision surfaced again in his eyes. Ming Huayan gave a sudden expression of dawning realization and smiled: "The name 'Lan Seventh Young Master' resounds throughout the jianghu, but very few mention the given name Lan Canyin. I truly did not think of it at once."

"In Hua Province, then..." Ning Lang had not caught this exchange — he had already jumped to his feet in excitement, and then caught himself, realized he had behaved too freely in front of others, and immediately bowed his head, face burning scarlet red. "Ming...Sir Ming, Master Lie — many thanks. I'll be going now." He clasped his hands in farewell, then looked up at Ming Huayan, then at Lie Chifeng, gave a good-natured smile, and turned to go.

"You'd do better to hold onto those gold leaves and not spend them carelessly," Lie Chifeng said to Ning Lang's retreating back.

"Huh?" Ning Lang turned around, then nodded obediently. "Alright."

Once Ning Lang had vanished from sight, Ming Huayan rose and reached out to touch a white lotus blossom beyond the pavilion's railing. A faint smile drifted across his face. "He called me 'Sir Ming,' but he called you 'Master Lie.' How interesting."

The breeze passed through, and every lotus — green and white alike — swayed in graceful, undulating waves. The fragrance of lotus drifted lightly on the wind. The azure-robed man's robe stirred in the breeze, as though he had been born from the blossoms themselves.

"Ning Lang," Lie Chifeng was saying on the side, puzzled. "I wonder what he is to them."

Just then, a bird fell from the sky without warning and landed on Ming Huayan's shoulder. It was a hawk — white from beak to tail.

Ming Huayan raised his hand, and the white hawk dropped into his palm. He untied a small bamboo tube from the bird's leg, and at a gesture of his hand the hawk took wing again and was gone. He drew a tiny slip of paper from the tube, unrolled it, and read. His eyes and brows remained perfectly still — not a trace of feeling disturbed his expression.

"I'm leaving." Lie Chifeng had been turning the matter over without reaching an answer and finally gave it up. He rose, gave a wave of the hand, and walked out of the pavilion.

Ming Huayan glanced back, his face bearing that smile impossible to read as joy or sorrow. He held up the slip of paper. "'Biyue Honor Master' Sui Qinghan has returned the Biyue Flower to Shouling Palace on Ying Mountain."

"What concern is that of mine." Lie Chifeng's voice came back without so much as a turn of the head, his steps not slowing even slightly.

"When a master of the martial world abdicates, it is surely the foremost event in all the jianghu — how can you be so unconcerned?" Ming Huayan called after him, his tone gentle and entirely sincere.

"Not interested." The last word fell as Lie Chifeng's figure vanished among the layers of lotus leaves.

"Is there truly nothing in this world that interests you, aside from your blade?" Ming Huayan addressed the empty air before him.

After a moment, he lowered his eyes and looked at the slip of paper in his hand. The mist-filled eyes drifted softly shut, and the corners of his lips curved upward, blooming into a smile purer and more beautiful than any white lotus. His lips parted, almost to himself: "The people of the Demon Cult are nothing if not willful."

chapters.title: Chapter Two: A Son Like a Green Lotus (Part Two)
chapters.content:
The forty-fourth year of Yinghua.

Nothing shook the martial world more than the news that the "Biyue Honor Master," the man who commanded the Black Path — and also the leader of what the martial world called the Demon Cult, the "Sui Cult" — Sui Qinghan, had sent the Biyue Flower, the emblem of his authority over half the martial world, back to Shouling Palace on Ying Mountain. The act signified his voluntary abdication from the position of Biyue Honor Master. Under the rules established by the Grand Assembly of the Martial World, the Lanyin and Biyue were to rise and fall together — and so, the moment Sui Qinghan returned the Biyue Flower, his co-regent, the "Lanyin Order Master" Ming Kong, who had stood with him atop the martial world, simultaneously lost his authority over the White Path.

The return of the Biyue Flower to Shouling Palace struck the martial world like a great stone hurled into still water, sending waves crashing in every direction. Everyone was stunned — and privately, nearly everyone was delighted.

Over a hundred and sixty years had passed since the Lanyin and Biyue first came to rule the jianghu, and in all that time, supreme ruler had followed supreme ruler, yet apart from the original founders — the first-generation "White Wind and Black Feng" — and the second-generation "Martial Emperor" Han Pu, not a single one had stepped down of their own accord. "White Wind and Black Feng" had been able to withdraw in their prime because they were the kind of people who had always treated kingly power as worn-out sandals and wealth as passing clouds. Those two were the only ones in all of history who had stirred the storms of a chaotic world and commanded the heroes of the jianghu before departing with a carefree wave. As for Martial Emperor Han Pu, he only retired in his twilight years, and had held sole dominion over the martial world for a full twenty years.

The throne of the martial world's sovereign — the power of life and death, the heroes of all the world at one's feet, what glory and honor — who could be unmoved? The positions of Lanyin Order Master and Biyue Honor Master had always been coveted by all, won only through blood and sweat, and defended at the cost of one's life. How could anyone abandon such a seat after only five short years? When Sui Qinghan had fought for the Biyue Flower back then, had he not also endured every hardship, bled every drop? Then why, in the very prime of his life, had he sent the flower back?

Beyond shock and speculation, nearly every heart harbored a quiet thrill.

The selection of a new supreme ruler of the martial world was at hand — perhaps this time, my chance has come!

And yet...

Worry began to creep in as well. Would the "Lanyin Order Master" Ming Kong truly relinquish his position? Would he be willing? What would he do next? After all, throughout history, the only way an Order Master had ever left his position was through death.

While the entire jianghu was buzzing with speculation about whether Ming Kong would voluntarily surrender the position of Order Master, news came down from Ying Mountain: the Lanyin and Biyue had reunited in the palace.

When this news spread, the jianghu erupted, and heroes everywhere leapt for joy.

Ming Kong had truly returned the Lanyin Order to Shouling Palace? But no one cared anymore about his reasons for doing so.

A new supreme ruler of the martial world was to be chosen! That was the first thought of every person who heard the news.

This time — it ought to be my turn. Every man who considered himself a peerless hero flexed his fists and itched for the chance.

The Shouling Palace on Ying Mountain stood waiting, its seat empty, and heroes far and wide rose to contend for it — another time of winds and surging clouds, another tide of rising heroes, another unknown count of bold spirits rushing forward, another unknown count of lives bled dry.

At that very moment, the young master of the Lan family was reclining on a beauty's lap, sipping the finest wine — a delicacy called "Rouge Drunk" — and listening with languid ease to the reports of his subordinates.

And Ning Lang, at a roadside inn, ran into someone who took it upon themselves to fill that honest, uncomplicated head of his with a dose of jianghu common sense — explaining to him what the rise and fall of the martial world meant, what the vicissitudes of the jianghu were, what great shifts in fortune and peril looked like, who qualified as a true hero... Whether any of it actually lodged itself in Ning Lang's mind, however, was a matter known only to heaven.

Even as the entire jianghu was in turmoil over the Lanyin and Biyue, and countless men were itching to try their luck, there were some who went about their days as before — watching the lone wild duck and the setting sun fly together, admiring the autumn river stretching wide and clear to meet the evening sky.

In the blink of an eye, the seventh month arrived. From the start of the month, martial folk had been making their way into Hua Province one after another, all heading toward the direction of Tianzhi Mountain.

Tianzhi Mountain was a celebrated place of scenic beauty — ancient stories of extraordinary romance, a landscape of quiet, ancient grandeur — and for a thousand years it had drawn travelers from near and far. At the foot of Tianzhi Mountain stood Longsky Manor, whose master, Qiu Changtian, was renowned throughout the jianghu for a palm technique called "Sky-Filling Palm," and was also known by the honorific "Scholar Hero" — for he was not only an outstanding martial artist but a man of learning and refined bearing, and the undisputed leader of the White Path in Hua Province.

But those now making their way to Longsky Manor were not there for the "Sky-Filling Palm."

Everyone in the jianghu knew that the Lanyin Biyue was the sacred token of the martial world's supreme ruler — but before it became that, it was a flower. It was a bloom cultivated by Feng Lanxi, King of the Feng Kingdom, over eight painstaking years, every ounce of his heart poured into it for the Wind Queen Feng Xiyun. It was the testament to a love that moved heaven and earth, the one tangible keepsake left to the world from that legendary tale. In its original form, it was a living flower that bloomed and faded with the seasons — but the sacred token was carved from the rarest jade, a replica in stone. The true Lanyin Biyue, the real flower of flesh and petal, had vanished from the world along with the departure of "White Wind and Black Feng," and for over a hundred years, countless people had tried to grow another — and all remained on that long, endless road, still searching.

In the middle of the seventh month, those who came to Longsky Manor came for a flower housed within the manor.

More than twenty years ago, Qiu Changtian had just taken a beautiful bride, and the two — equally talented, equally fine of character — were deeply devoted to each other, the envy of many a couple throughout the jianghu. Qiu's wife was also a person of the jianghu and knew well the story of the Lanyin Biyue. One evening in those early days of marriage, gazing at the moon together and admiring the blossoms, she had sighed that the world would never again see the beauty of the Lanyin Biyue — just as the world could never again produce a second pair of "White Wind and Black Feng." Qiu Changtian, confident that his love for his wife was no less than that of those legendary figures, immediately made her a solemn promise: he would grow a Lanyin Biyue of his own, as proof of his devotion.

It had taken Feng Lanxi eight years to grow the Lanyin Biyue. It took Qiu Changtian eighteen years — and in the end, he did grow a flower. The tragedy was that it bloomed nine years too late. Qiu's wife had already been silent in her grave, and moreover, the flower he grew was not the Lanyin Biyue.

No one had ever seen the true Lanyin Biyue in the flesh, but from what was written about it one could know: it grew from a single stem that bore two blooms, one black and one white — the white flower with dark stamens, the black with snow-white stamens, the petals shaped like crescent moons, luminous as jade and as radiant as the moon. It was pure and elegant, yet also stately and dignified — much like its creators.

The flower Qiu Changtian grew, however, was entirely white, and bore only one bloom per stem. Its singularity lay in the petals — not the crescent-moon shape of the Lanyin Biyue, but half-moon shaped, each one curving open alongside the last, until together they formed a perfect full circle, ring joined to ring, completing a round, full moon.

Qiu Changtian later named this flower the "Banyin" — half of "Lanyin," half of a good marriage: a once-beautiful hope that had ended in solitary sorrow.

Yet even so, though it was not the Lanyin Biyue, the flower's singular, exquisite beauty had made the name "Banyin" known far and wide. Add to that the story of Qiu Changtian's devoted effort, and countless hearts were moved. It could be called the second most famous flower after the Lanyin Biyue itself. With so many admirers came the desire to grow one — to have it at home, both for enjoyment and as a point of pride. Strangely, transplanted Banyin never lasted more than five days before wilting, and seeds buried in soil were as impotent as stones, no matter how carefully watered and fertilized, never sending up a single sprout. Yet the Banyin in Longsky Manor bloomed faithfully every year, like snow, like moonlight.

Every seventh month was the time for the Banyin to bloom. During that season, the entire manor was wrapped in its fragrance, and those who came to "admire the flowers" — as they grandly called it — multiplied. Jianghu folk, for all their lives spent amid blades and blood, were not without some capacity to cherish beauty — and some were great pretenders to refined taste as well.

Perhaps at the start it truly was only for the Banyin, but as years passed, the gathering took on a different flavor.

Jianghu people, however they might love flowers, loved martial skill more — so after admiring the blooms they would often linger instead of leaving, and put questions of kung fu to Qiu Changtian. And Qiu Changtian, bearing the title "Scholar Hero," was outstanding in both literary and martial arts.
