None of those who came looking for advantage gained any — they left instead with their tails between their legs. Some, however, found themselves won over and asked to learn in earnest. Being the kind of man Qiu Changtian was — in character, in virtue, in talent, in skill — he never turned away a sincere question, and actively encouraged the younger generation to set aside their sectarian biases and challenge and learn from one another. Many who returned home afterward made notable advances in their martial arts, no small number of them going on to achieve real accomplishment. Before long, people throughout the jianghu began to regard an invitation to Longsky Manor as an honor. And so it became a tradition: every seventh month, martial folk would make their own way to Longsky Manor, some to see the magnificent rare flower, others to receive guidance from a senior master and spar with peers — all striving to advance on the path of martial arts. The Seventh Month at Longsky had become a small festival of the martial world — nothing like the grand, thundering, blood-stirring spectacle of the Grand Assembly at Ying Mountain, but something leisurely and freely chosen, a gathering of friends through the shared language of martial skill, with far less of the killing and the bloodshed.

But in recent years, those who came to Longsky Manor had arrived with another motive as well — and the ranks of the young grew notably larger.

The forty-fourth year of Yinghua, the seventh month.

Longsky Manor again welcomed many friends from the jianghu, as it had every year. And at the foot of Tianzhi Mountain, new inns and restaurants had opened in recent years, prospering handsomely in the manor's shadow. Every seventh month they were filled to capacity, their staff running ragged, their proprietors dazzled by the gleam of silver.

For though Longsky Manor was a martial world family of means and wanted for nothing in the way of food or comfort, feeding and housing so many jianghu guests every year would exhaust even the largest family fortune. And so Qiu Changtian had long since made it publicly clear: all were welcome to come to Longsky Manor for the flowers and for martial discussion — but guests were expected to see to their own food and lodging. Only those who received a personal invitation from Qiu Changtian himself could stay within the manor. All others took rooms at the inns outside. The outer courtyard's Banyin flowers were open for viewing at any time, but entry into the inner courtyard for martial discussion was restricted to a single day: the sixteenth day of the seventh month.

At last the sixteenth arrived. The gates of Longsky Manor's inner courtyard were thrown open at the hour of mao, and the manor's chief steward was already at the door, standing ready to welcome the jianghu heroes as they arrived.

By tradition, the gathering did not officially begin until the hour of chen, when Qiu Changtian would appear to greet his guests — sometimes accompanied by a few invited friends as well. In truth, the atmosphere of the manor gathering was nothing like the grave, tension-filled spectacle the outside world imagined. It was more a matter of everyone sitting together, talking about what they had recently learned, what difficulties they had encountered, what insights they had gained on their martial path — with some challenging each other in friendly bouts, everyone discussing, testing, solving, and sharing. Qiu Changtian himself never stood on the dignity of his reputation as an elder master. His words were warm, his learning broad and deep, and he treated every person — old and young, famous and obscure, highly skilled and still beginning — with exactly the same respect. To any question anyone put to him, he would answer without reservation, doing his best to advise, and if there was something he himself had not yet worked out, he said so plainly and honestly. He also often shared his own discoveries with everyone — and those discoveries were never limited to the martial path alone. Those who had attended in past years would not soon forget the afternoon in the forty-first year of Yinghua when he had hung up an ink-painted scroll of bamboo, beaming with delight, insisting on sharing the joy of it with all present.

That day, starting from the hour of mao, jianghu guests arrived one by one and passed through the inner courtyard gate, each hoping to claim a good spot from which to see and hear clearly. As people filed in and looked about, they could not help but silently admire what they saw.

The courtyard was spacious and generously laid out — water pavilions and cool gazebos, ornamental rockeries and flat stones, small alcoves and winding covered walkways, all arranged with quiet, ingenious precision. But what drew the most delighted surprise were the seats. In the water pavilion, bamboo chairs caught the breeze; in the gazebos, stone benches cooled to the touch; on the flat rocks, woven reed mats had been spread; inside the alcoves, small low tables were set close together; along the covered walkways, reclining couches had been placed here and there; and the snow-white Banyin blossoms nodded on stone steps and wooden railings, standing slender and graceful on every terrace and promontory. The whole scene left the guests with dazzled eyes and hearts full of pleasure.

Once everyone had found a seat, they looked about again and found a scene as fine as a painting. Some chairs were arranged side by side in rows, others gathered in clusters of three or five, some in pairs facing each other, and some set alone for a single quiet occupant. The Banyin flowers dotted the scene like wheel after wheel of snow-white moonlight, their perfect faces turned toward the guests on every side.

In that moment, even the roughest and most unrefined of jianghu heroes felt a stirring of quiet, otherworldly elegance — as though one dwelt within the moon, and the moon dwelt within oneself. The morning air was light and cool, a faint, clean fragrance drifting all around. It felt like a garden out of a dream. All striving ambition dissolved in an instant, and one thought only: to be here like this — faced with such beauty, in perfect harmony of spirit, drinking freely, speaking of heaven's height and the sea's depth, talking of the heroes this world has known — that, truly, would be the finest pleasure life could offer.

Whose brilliant and clever hands had arranged all this? Every person present silently asked themselves.

In years past the inner courtyard had simply held everyone gathered around in a circle. Nothing had ever been done quite like this before. The guests were both delighted and thankful — delighted by the charming, original arrangement, and grateful they had not missed it.

This year's gathering would certainly surpass every year before it.

chapters.title: Chapter Two: A Son Like a Green Lotus (Part Three)
chapters.content:
Time always slips away without a sound.

When the morning sun spilled down in brilliant gold and gilded the Banyin blossoms with a layer of warm radiance, the hour of chen was nearly upon them. Most of those attending had arrived, and the gate had seen no one cross it for some time. The chief steward was just about to give the order to close the manor doors when he caught sight of two distant figures running toward him at full tilt.

"Wait! Wait for us!"

Someone was shouting as they ran. In no time at all, the two had reached the gate.

"We made it... just in time!" One of them leaned against the doorframe, catching his breath, while the other wiped the sweat from his brow, gave the manor guards a slightly abashed smile, and breathed easily — not a trace of fatigue about him. It was plain that this one's stamina and inner energy far exceeded his companion's.

"May I ask the names of the two young heroes?" The chief steward standing at the gate clasped his hands in greeting.

"Thank you, thank you." The one who had been gasping finally caught his breath, clasped his hands with a grateful smile for not having been shut out, and looked up with a wide, open grin, revealing two sharp little canine teeth. Thick brows, large eyes — not particularly handsome, but a face that put people at ease the moment they saw it. The one beside him was slightly younger, his features striking and upright, with a pair of steady, dark eyes full of vigor.

"Please, there is no need for thanks." The manor guards quickly returned the greeting. The people of the Qiu household, from the master down to the guards, were unfailingly courteous.

"I am Yuwen Luo, and this is my sworn brother Ning Lang. We have come hoping to attend the Senior Qiu's 'Banyin Forum on Swords' — if we may..."Yuwen Luo stretched his neck to look past the gate as he spoke.

Banyin Forum on Swords? The steward and guards exchanged a startled glance. Many people came to the gathering every year, but no one had ever thought to give it a name — and the master himself, for all his literary talent, had never considered it either. This young Yuwen hero had only just arrived and already coined a name for it. But "Banyin Forum on Swords" actually sounded quite good.

"All who come are guests. How could we possibly refuse?" The steward waved a hand and welcomed both men inside.

"Ning Lang, come on — we're going in!" Yuwen Luo grabbed Ning Lang by the arm and strode through the gate.

Once inside the courtyard, both men paused in admiration at the scene of flowers and people in perfect harmony.

"Wonderful, wonderful, wonderful — the flowers are extraordinary, the people are heroes. A fine pairing, not one at odds with the other." Yuwen Luo exclaimed again and again. "I knew I had named it right — 'Banyin Forum on Swords.'"

The heroes gathered in the courtyard turned at the sound, glanced toward the gate, saw two unfamiliar young men with nothing particularly remarkable about them, and looked away again.

"Big Brother, it looks like every seat is taken." Ning Lang scanned the courtyard uneasily, feeling the press of all those eyes. There did seem to be no empty spaces left.

"Hmm..." Yuwen Luo's large eyes swept the grounds, then suddenly lit up. "There's still one spot — the best one in the whole courtyard."

"Where?" Ning Lang craned his neck for another look. He was right — every seat in the garden was occupied, except for the small pavilion in the very center, which was clearly being held for the host.

"Follow me." Yuwen Luo crooked his finger and started forward. Ning Lang was puzzled but followed along.

"Look — no one here at all, and the best view in the whole courtyard," said Yuwen Luo, pointing ahead with great self-satisfaction.

Before them was an ornamental rockery.

"Is this... really alright?" Ning Lang looked at the rockery and then at Yuwen Luo.

"Of course it is," Yuwen Luo said with confidence. "This rockery is on the eastern side and it's purely decorative — not very tall at all. We climb up top and we can see the whole courtyard. Perfect."

"But..." Ning Lang still hesitated.

Yuwen Luo was already up, having leapt onto the rockery in a single bound. He settled into a crouch, looked around, and confirmed: yes, the entire courtyard spread out before him in perfect clarity. He beckoned to Ning Lang. "Get up here."

Seeing that Yuwen Luo had already sat himself down, Ning Lang leapt up as well. Looking out, he had to admit it was exactly as described — a "perfect view." Not only was the whole gathering below in full sight, but even half the surrounding buildings of Longsky Manor were visible.

"Goodness, there are a lot of people. So many of them are famous names in the jianghu — no wonder in recent years Tianzhi Mountain has started being mentioned in the same breath as Ying Mountain." Yuwen Luo swept his gaze carefully over the assembled heroes, marveling aloud.

"Big Brother, do you know all of them?" Ning Lang's gaze moved from face to face through the crowd below — not one did he recognize.

"Not know them." Yuwen Luo's eyes brightened a notch with each new face he landed on.

"Then how do you know they're all famous?"

"I may not have seen them, but I've heard of them." Yuwen Luo shot him a look. "Your Brother here has sworn to write a History of the Martial World that will live for a thousand years. How could I not know the famous figures of the jianghu? And knowing them isn't enough — I need to understand their backgrounds, their sects, their habits, and think through their martial skill and character thoroughly. Otherwise, how could I write a history of the martial world that future generations can only look up to with awe?"

"Oh." Ning Lang nodded.

Yuwen Luo turned his gaze back to the famous figures below, pulling out paper and brush from his chest. "It would be an embarrassment for the younger brother of a future great historian of the martial world to know nothing at all about the people of the jianghu. You understand? So your Brother here has a duty to fill in some of the most basic jianghu common knowledge for you. First comes recognizing faces and knowing names. Now then..." He turned back. "Ning Lang, let your Brother test you. Name the great sects and clans of the martial world."

Ning Lang flushed slightly at the question, even simple as his thinking was. "Big Brother, I may be short on jianghu experience, but I do know about the sects," he said. After all, he had come from Qianbei Mountain, one of those very sects.

"Answer what I ask." Yuwen Luo tapped the brush handle against Ning Lang's forehead. "An older brother is like a father — you follow my lead."  Having always been the smallest at home, it felt good to finally have a younger brother of his own. He had to make the most of it.

Ning Lang rubbed his head with resignation, then answered dutifully: "Currently, the martial world is made up of one hundred and forty-seven sects, but at the top are the One Cult, Four Schools, and Six Great Families."

"Hmm." Yuwen Luo nodded approvingly, wearing the expression of a student who has not yet disappointed. "In detail."

"The One Cult is the Sui Cult. The Four Schools are Qianbei, Fengwu, Cangyun, and Taoluo. The Six Great Families are the Ming family of Tian Province, the Lan family of Yun Province, the Qiu family of Hua Province, the Hua family of Bai Province, the Yuwen family of Yue Province, and the Ning family of Lan Province." Ning Lang bent all ten fingers and counted them off one by one, afraid of making a mistake.

"Good. You know them all." Yuwen Luo gave another approving nod. He pressed the brush handle beneath Ning Lang's chin and turned his face toward the courtyard below. "Now your Brother will teach you to recognize people. This courtyard may not be the largest in the world, but it has gathered something close to every hero of the age."

There was still a trace of the childlike in Yuwen Luo's face — but his eyes were bright and sharp.

Just as the older Yuwen brother was settling in to give his younger Ning brother a proper lesson in famous jianghu figures, the courtyard — which had been pleasantly lively up until then — suddenly fell silent. Every person present turned to look in one direction. Yuwen Luo, whose calling in life was to witness and record all things great and small in the martial world, naturally would not miss an event that drew so much attention. He shifted his gaze and followed the crowd's line of sight — and what he saw made his soul nearly leave his body in fright. He couldn't run, not with everyone watching. If he drew the attention of that person, things would only get worse. He immediately pulled Ning Lang in front of himself, praying that person's eyes were not sharp enough to spot him through the crowd.

The Ning family's little brother sat there rigid and confused, looking back at the big Yuwen brother, utterly unable to explain why the man who had been holding forth with such confidence only a moment ago had suddenly turned into this cowering, cringing version of himself.

"Big Brother..."

"Shh — don't say a word." Yuwen Luo quickly pressed his hand over Ning Lang's mouth and lowered his voice. "Block me for a moment. Whatever you do, don't let anyone see me."

Ning Lang, his mouth and nose both covered, grew very uncomfortable. He nodded repeatedly, using his eyes to signal: let go, please, now.

Yuwen Luo released him, shrank in behind Ning Lang's back, and tried to make himself invisible. But he had chosen a "spot with a perfect view" — and on top of a rockery, anyone who turned their head or tilted their gaze upward at all would immediately see two people sitting up there. Ning Lang himself looked quite openly toward the person now entering the courtyard — whoever it was that had frightened his big brother so badly.

Five people had arrived. Two elders walked at the front, side by side, both appearing to be around fifty years of age. One wore a plain white cloth and homespun robe, his bearing refined and elegant, his gaze calm yet carrying a quiet, undemonstrative authority. The other had a lean face and three long wisps of beard, a master's air about him from head to toe. Behind them followed three young men: one slightly stout and cheerful-looking with a warm smile on his face, one tall and handsome but cold and haughty in expression, and one of fine, delicate features whose head was slightly bowed as though lost in thought. This group of five was the sort of people who inspired only respect and goodwill on sight — nothing about them should have frightened Yuwen Luo like this.

As the five entered the courtyard, every person seated within — old and young alike — rose to clasp their hands and bow to the two elders at the front, and called out greetings to the three young men behind them. For a moment the courtyard filled with the voices of people exchanging courtesies and introductions. The two figures perched on the rockery were conspicuously motionless through all of this. As the others resettled into their seats, the cold and haughty young man, who had stepped into the small central pavilion, suddenly turned around, and his gaze swept directly and unhesitatingly toward the rockery. In that instant, Ning Lang felt as though he had been struck by an arrow — he could not have moved a muscle if he tried.

The cold, haughty young man raised his hand. His index finger crooked once.

Was he... calling me over? Ning Lang blinked. He had no idea who this person was.

The finger crooked again.

Is he really calling me? Ning Lang shifted, about to rise — but a pair of hands clamped down hard on him from behind. "He can't see me, he can't see me, he can't see me..." a monotonous, prayer-like murmur buzzed steadily in his ear.

"Big Brother..."

"Shh — not a sound." Yuwen Luo immediately pressed a hand over Ning Lang's face, lowering his voice further. "Just block me for a minute — don't let anyone see me."

Ning Lang's mouth and nose were covered and he was deeply uncomfortable. He kept nodding, using his eyes to plead: let go already.

Yuwen Luo released him, hunched down behind Ning Lang, trying to disappear. But the "spot with a perfect view" was exactly that — anyone who glanced up or turned their head would immediately see two figures sitting on top of the rockery. Ning Lang, for his part, was looking openly at whoever was entering — he wanted to know what kind of person could frighten his big brother like this.

"Yuwen Luo!" A voice rang out — carrying the faintest note of warning — and the gaze of everyone in the courtyard turned at once toward the cold and haughty young man, then followed his eyes up to the rockery.

The shout startled Ning Lang — and clarified things: the man was calling his sworn brother, not him.

"I am going to lose a layer of skin over this," came Yuwen Luo's wretched murmur from behind him. Then the grip on his collar loosened, and Yuwen Luo jumped down from the rockery.

"Big Brother..." Ning Lang hesitated, unsure whether to follow.

"Get down." Yuwen Luo beckoned with a drooping hand and began his slow, reluctant trudge toward the small central pavilion.

Ning Lang thought briefly, then jumped down and fell in step behind Yuwen Luo. Sworn brothers should share both hardship and fortune.

"Big Brother." When they reached the small pavilion, Yuwen Luo greeted the cold, haughty young man with a subdued obedience. Behind him, Ning Lang was genuinely startled — this...person was Big Brother's big brother? They looked nothing alike.

The cold young man let a faint smile cross his face, walked to Yuwen Luo, and rested a hand on his shoulder in an easy, brotherly way. "Fifth Brother, you're here too." He lowered his head, a quiet, measured sentence dropping straight into Yuwen Luo's ear: "Don't embarrass the Yuwen family in public. I'll settle accounts with you later."

Yuwen Luo raised his head, his face all smiles, those little sharp canine teeth making him look all the more endearing. He turned into the small pavilion, clasped his hands, and bowed deeply. "Yuwen Luo presents himself to Senior Qiu and Senior Nan."

"This is my fifth younger brother," said the cold young man, stepping back into the pavilion as well.

"So this is the fifth son of the Yuwen family," the lean elder with the three-strand beard said, smoothing his whiskers with a slight nod.

"Young Yuwen need not stand on ceremony." The refined, scholarly elder smiled warmly, then looked toward Ning Lang, who still stood outside the pavilion looking uneasy. "Is the young man outside a friend of yours?"

"That is my sworn brother, Ning Lang. Like myself, he has come in admiration of the Senior's chivalrous renown, hoping to pay his respects." Yuwen Luo answered with polished courtesy, then turned to beckon Ning Lang. "Ning Lang, this is the master of Longsky Manor, Senior Qiu Changtian." He shifted his gaze to the lean elder with the three-strand beard. "And this is the sect master of Taoluo Gate, Senior Nan Wofeng."

"Junior Ning Lang pays his respects to both seniors." Ning Lang immediately stepped forward to bow.

Nan Wofeng gave an approving nod. Qiu Changtian's gaze skimmed over the silver spear across Ning Lang's back — the spear was half the length of an ordinary one, roughly the length of a sword.

"How is Brother Ning Mo these days?"

"Ah..." Ning Lang blinked, then answered, "He is well." This person knew his father?

"Good." Qiu Changtian smiled and nodded.

On the other side, Yuwen Luo had already exchanged greetings with the other two young men.

"Qiu Zang." Qiu Changtian called his chief steward. "Have seats arranged for the two young gentlemen."

"Oh — please don't trouble yourself, Senior Qiu," Yuwen Luo quickly objected. "Your junior can find a spot anywhere — there is no need to put the senior to any trouble." Sitting here with them would be like sitting on a bed of nails.

"Ha..." Qiu Changtian looked at Yuwen Luo with a soft laugh, then instructed the steward, "Set them up at the rockery."

At these words, Yuwen Luo let out a very obvious breath of relief. He turned to look at the eldest Yuwen son, Yuwen Feng. "Big Brother, I'll head over there now."

"Go." Yuwen Feng nodded once.

Yuwen Luo gave a nod to each person in the pavilion, then led Ning Lang out to the rockery, where a table and chairs had already been set with a pot of tea, two cups, and two small dishes of refreshments.

They had barely sat down when Qiu Changtian's voice began to ring out across the courtyard: "To have so many friends from the jianghu gather here honors Qiu deeply. I must confess, however, that in recent years I have made little progress on the martial path — to my great shame before all of you." His voice paused for a moment, and several voices rose immediately to say he was being too modest. He waved a hand and swept his gaze over the courtyard before continuing: "There is a saying: the Yangtze's rear waves drive the ones before. The jianghu today is full of outstanding young heroes — the days of rising winds and turning clouds all belong to them. Yet ordinarily we so rarely have the chance to meet. Today, with so many gathered under one roof, Qiu finds himself quite moved, and would very much like to see the spirit of the new jianghu firsthand. I wonder what the gathered friends here think?"

Put simply, this meant: today, all the elders stand aside and let the younger generation show what they can do. And so when the words landed, bright, eager light immediately filled every young pair of eyes in the courtyard. To win first place here at Longsky Manor — among this gathering, with heroes from every direction — would mean being known as the foremost talent of the younger generation. What glory that would be!

"Yes!"

The younger generation immediately broke into cheering, while the elders, having no desire to lower themselves to compete, all smiled and nodded along.

Qiu Changtian swept his gaze once more over the full courtyard of heroes, smiling. "Before the young heroes display their abilities, there is something Qiu would like to share with everyone."

"Junior arrived late — would Senior Qiu be willing to let me share in it as well?" A voice drifted in suddenly from outside the courtyard.

chapters.title: Chapter Three: The Grand Gathering at Longsky (Part One)
chapters.content:
That voice made every person think of a still, dark pool on a moonlit night — the cool, clear shimmer of reflected light, soft ripples spreading outward in rings, a fatal and irresistible pull.

Then the manor gates opened wide, and that person simply walked in, unhurried and unburdened, as though treading across still water.

Ink-black hair bound beneath a golden crown, white hair ribbons drifting at the shoulders, a deep purple robe with wide, flowing sleeves, brows like brushstrokes of dark ink, and set into that jade face — a pair of uncommon jade-green eyes. A single, light sweep of those eyes, and every heart in the courtyard gave a start — followed immediately by a sensation that could not quite be named: a tremor of dread.

The person stood there, smiled gently, tapped a white jade fan shut, and bowed with clasped hands. "Junior Lan Qi pays his respects to the elders."

In a courtyard full of Banyin blossoms white as moon and snow, the air heavy with that cool, clear beauty — yet in that single instant, it was as though a thousand crimson peonies had burst into bloom all at once, their blazing color seizing every gaze.

The entire courtyard held its breath. Souls drifted.

A moment later, Ning Lang came back to himself and tugged at Yuwen Luo's sleeve, pointing at the object of everyone's stunned attention. "He... he is..."

But at this moment, Yuwen Luo had no attention to spare.

Paper — shimmering with a silver sheen — brush unlike wolf-hair, its tip fine as a needle, moving rapidly, carefully carving out a line of small formal script: In the forty-fourth year of Yinghua, on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, first encounter with Lan Qi at Longsky Manor. His radiance seized the souls of all present.

"Big Brother, I know this person," Ning Lang said with great excitement.

"What?" That woke Yuwen Luo up as well. "You actually know the famous Lan Qi?!"

"I saw him in Yuzhou — he even gave me seven gold leaves!" Ning Lang's eyes were bright as stars.

"What?!" Yuwen Luo's eyes blazed. "He gave you gold leaves? What is your connection to him? How did you come to know each other? Did you know who he was at the time? What did he say to you? What did he do? Why would he give anything to you..." 

This torrent of questions left Ning Lang's younger brother at a loss.

"I..." The younger Ning brother opened his mouth but found no words. How did one even begin to describe meeting Lan Qi?

"Speak!" Yuwen Luo urged.

"I... who exactly is Lan Qi?" Rather than answering the question, Ning Lang pressed out a puzzlement that had been lodged in his chest for some time.

Yuwen Luo stared at him, then slapped his own forehead. "How could I expect anything from you!"

"Big Brother..."

"Shh — watch first." Yuwen Luo pointed toward the small central pavilion.

"So it is the Seventh Young Master — quite an unexpected honor." Qiu Changtian rose from the pavilion with a face full of smiles to come out and greet him.

Nan Wofeng also stepped out of the pavilion, a rare smile softening the thin and weathered face. "This old man would never have imagined the Seventh Young Master would come in person."

Lan Qi's jade fan swayed lightly. "Junior has long heard of the Longsky gathering and always wished to attend. Coming uninvited this time — I only hope the seniors will forgive the presumption."

"Seventh Young Master is too modest. Your coming honors this humble gate. Please, right this way." Qiu Changtian swept a hand to invite Lan Qi into the pavilion and took his seat, while Qiu Zang the steward had already had someone bring an additional chair without needing to be told.

"Many thanks."

The three were just about to enter the pavilion when the three young men already seated inside rose to receive Lan Qi — and at that moment, a voice drifted in again from beyond the gate.

"Junior arrived late — I wonder if Senior Qiu would allow Huayan to enter and witness this occasion?"

That voice was spring wind and summer rain — warm and clear and refreshing.

"It is the Second Young Master of the Ming family! Please, come in quickly!" The refined expression on Qiu Changtian's face had now given way to undisguised delight. And he was not alone — the entire courtyard had risen, every gaze fixed on the gate.

First, a corner of blue robe drifted in. Then a tall, upright figure walked forward at an unhurried pace — features of fine, serene elegance, a faint smile at the corner of his lips. The fragrance that had filled the courtyard until now was Banyin blossoms, but as he walked through, it seemed instead to carry with it the cool, understated scent of green lotus. His gaze moved lightly across the crowd, misty and distant, as though seen from across the water.

Azure robes drifting, he clasped his hands and bowed. "Junior Ming Huayan pays his respects to the two seniors."

"Please, young master, there is no need." Qiu Changtian moved quickly to help him up.

"I would never have imagined that today even the Second Young Master of the Ming family would come," said Nan Wofeng, stroking his beard with a smile. He looked toward Qiu Changtian. "Brother Changtian, your face truly carries great weight."

"To have this many young heroes come today — Qiu is truly overjoyed beyond expectation." Qiu Changtian nodded repeatedly. "Come — let me make introductions." He turned first to introduce Lan Qi. "Second Young Master, this is the seventh young master of the Lan family, Lan Qi. Seventh Young Master, this is the second young master of the Ming family."

The two stepped forward to exchange greetings. Their eyes met — and both gave a slight start.

The eyes across from him were jade-green and deeply unfathomable, clear ripples concealing something within.

The eyes before him were bright yet shrouded in mist, their boundless warmth clearly guarding something as well.

"Demon."

"Fake immortal."

Both spoke at precisely the same instant — a burst of instinct that bypassed all reason, impossible to control. The moment each realized what they had said, they found every eye in the courtyard wide with shock and dismay.

"Ah, so you are the Second Young Master of the Ming family — I have long admired your name."

"The Seventh Young Master's fame has reached my ears like thunder."

The two speakers, however, had already recovered. The rest of the courtyard was still blinking in stunned silence as both stepped forward with easy composure, smiling at each other. Just as everyone expected them to clasp hands in warm greeting, those half-extended hands turned subtly mid-gesture and returned to their owners' sides without a trace.

"To meet the Second Young Master today truly is a stroke of extraordinary fortune."

"Not at all — I have long admired the Seventh Young Master."

Both bowed to each other, each sneaking a glance at the other. Hmm... the face is familiar, somehow. Where had they seen it before?

The rest of the courtyard, seeing how warmly they seemed to regard each other, convinced themselves they must have misheard. The shock dissolved, and people came forward one by one — those who knew them offering greetings, those who didn't seizing the chance to introduce themselves to the two most celebrated young figures in the martial world today. Only Yuwen Luo was carefully writing those two phrases into his newly opened History of the Martial World — phrases that would later be praised as the most precise and vivid "epithets" ever coined.

As for Qiu Changtian and Nan Wofeng, those two men of deep virtue and high standing, they exchanged a glance, then let the matter go with a serene smile, taking the outburst as nothing more than the impulsive exclamation of two young men who, on meeting a true equal, found themselves gripped by wariness and excitement in equal measure. They thought no more of it, and turned instead to introduce the three young men already seated within the pavilion.

"Big Brother, those two people..." Ning Lang pointed toward the center of the crowd with great humility. "Who are they? Why does everyone treat them with such deference?"

Ning Lang, simple as his understanding of people and social situations was, could still read the room well enough to sense that the weight these two carried seemed, if anything, to exceed that of the two great masters, Qiu Changtian and Nan Wofeng.

"Ah." Yuwen Luo looked at Ning Lang heavily and sighed a deep sigh. "You came from Qianbei Mountain, one of the Four Great Schools, and you are the young heir of the Ning family, one of the Six Great Clans — and yet you do not know these people, whose names should make any person of the jianghu tremble with awe the moment they hear them. Truly, I don't know what to say to you. Fortunately...fortunately, you met me."

"Big Brother." The younger Ning brother had been talked into feeling a little ashamed, and scratched his head. "Master said that on the path of martial arts, one must focus the heart and still the mind, and not be swayed by the outside world. So I..."

"So you took that old man's words literally, buried yourself in practice, cared nothing for the world beyond, and turned yourself into a complete blockhead!" Yuwen Luo gave the top of his little brother's head a smack, looking thoroughly exasperated, as if faced with wood past carving. "Truly a simple-minded child."

"Big Brother, you still haven't told me." Ning Lang scratched his head again, his gaze wandering back toward the two most striking figures in the courtyard.

"Lan Qi, the current head of the Lan family of Yun Province..." Yuwen Luo pointed at the person in the purple robe with the jade-green eyes.

"Ah, so he is from the Lan family of Yun Province..." Ning Lang exclaimed.

"Be quiet!" The big Yuwen brother was very displeased at being interrupted mid-sentence. "No interrupting when I'm speaking!"

Ning Lang's mouth moved, but under the force of Yuwen Luo's rather imposing glare, he swallowed whatever he was going to say.

"Ahem." The big Yuwen brother cleared his throat with dignity, then put on a serious expression. "Though the Lan family had made its name in the martial world for some time, they truly secured their place of real importance only after this Seventh Young Master here took over as family head. He was fourteen when he was given the position — skipping his parents' generation entirely, receiving it directly from the previous head of the Lan family, his grandfather. After that, many among the Lan family's senior and junior lineages died or departed, quite a number of them, in fact — the family shrank considerably. Yet Lan's power and influence only grew, and today stands as one of the Six Great Families at the very top of the martial world. As for the matter of the Lan family members dying off one after another, the rumor in the jianghu is that he was responsible. But that is only rumor and cannot be trusted — I, as a fair and impartial historian of the martial world, am still investigating the true circumstances. What I will say, however, is that I find him genuinely admirable."

He paused for a moment, pleased to see that the younger Ning brother was listening attentively, then continued: "The Lan family is a long-established name in the martial world, with roots nearly a hundred years deep, branches and tendrils everywhere, and a lineage full of formidable people. No one born into that house is a simple individual — and yet he seized the head's position from that entire pack of wolves and tigers at only fourteen years of age. Ah..." He shook his head in quiet awe. "Not to mention what he did after taking charge of the family — a few incidents that truly made the whole jianghu shudder. The Lan family's dominance over Yun Province today is entirely to this Seventh Young Master's credit." As he said this, he stole a glance at the person with that smile capable of bewitching the world, and his own heart gave a little clench.

"To speak of the timeline: from the day he became family head to now has been roughly six or seven years. He made his name very early, but for the first few years he was known only by reputation — his actual appearance in the jianghu is really only a matter of the last two years. The Lan family is an orthodox clan, but this Seventh Young Master's way of doing things is neither wholly orthodox nor wholly unorthodox. And there are rumors of ties between him and the Demon Cult that run deep. Last and most important of all is his appearance — incomparable in this world, and yet gifted with a pair of jade-green eyes that carry an unmistakable air of the demonic. Which is why the jianghu treats him with reverence and fear in equal measure — people want to get close and yet dare not approach too near. A contradiction in every sense. If he were willing to be my friend, though, I would be very happy about that."

Yuwen Luo had said a great deal. He poured himself a cup of tea and wet his throat, then looked at Ning Lang. "You know who he is now?"

Ning Lang looked at Lan Qi, then back at Yuwen Luo, and nodded. "The formidable head of the martial world clan, the Lan family."

"Not bad — a decent summary." Yuwen Luo accepted this with considerable pride, and raised his hand to point at the person dressed in azure blue, still as a lotus. "The Second Young Master of the Ming family — Ming Huayan — is the young heir of the Ming family of Tian Province. If Lan Qi is someone people regard with both dread and reverence, then Ming Er is someone people hold with both reverence and love. The Ming family has produced three Lanyin Order Masters — the very first one came from their line, over a hundred years ago — and their standing in the martial world is absolutely first among all. As for this Second Young Master of the Ming family... how to put it..." Yuwen Luo propped his chin on a bent finger and thought for a long while, and at last exhaled a quiet sigh. "Perhaps only the name the jianghu has given him does him any justice: 'Banished Immortal' — an immortal banished to the mortal realm. A figure of the divine. What could a mere mortal like me possibly presume to say?"

Ning Lang looked over at that description, at the otherworldly face and those eyes that seemed to gaze from beyond ten thousand mountains — and had to admit, only the words "Banished Immortal" could do justice to such a person.

"Speaking of names, Lan Qi has one too — and it is no less fitting than Ming Er's title. Do you know what it is?" Yuwen Luo asked with a secretive smile.

Ning Lang shook his head, as was only natural.

"Jade Demon!" Yuwen Luo declared the name softly but with great weight.

"Ah?" Ning Lang listened with a twinge of indignation.

"Ha — a son of a great clan, addressed by the word 'demon.' Anyone else would have had the mouth of whoever spread the name sewn shut. But this Seventh Young Master welcomed it gladly." Yuwen Luo's eyes lit with amusement. "He even said: 'The greatest wish of my life is to become a demon — ten thousand forms, commanding wind and rain, immortal and undying, drinking deep of every last pleasure this world has to offer.'"

"But..."

"'But that name carries an insult' — is that what you were going to say?" Yuwen Luo cut him off.

Ning Lang nodded. He did not know why, but something in him utterly refused to accept that this person should be called by a name meant to demean.

"To turn a name meant to shame into something beautiful — is that not the mark of someone capable of what ordinary people cannot?" Yuwen Luo said with a smile, shifting his gaze to the one who bore that demonic name yet seemed to exhale, faintly and with complete ease, a trace of something genuinely otherworldly. His voice dropped almost to nothing. "Ning Lang — do you think we'll live to see the day? When being called a demon becomes something everyone takes pride in." There was, beneath the lightness of those words, a seriousness that was not quite easy to detect.

After a round of greetings among the assembled guests, everyone returned to their seats. It was Lan Qi who spoke first. "I wonder what precious thing Senior Qiu has in mind to share with us today?"

Qiu Changtian smiled and glanced at Qiu Zang, who stood beside him. Qiu Zang caught the signal at once: a raised hand, and three manor servants walked out into the courtyard. The one at the front carried a long rectangular tray covered with a red silk cloth.

"With the Lanyin Biyue returned to Shouling Palace and the Grand Assembly on Ying Mountain approaching, Qiu is too old to contend for it himself — but this is precisely the moment for all of you young heroes to show what you are made of. Today, with so many gathered under this one roof, Qiu was suddenly struck with a whim: to have a first glimpse of these heroes' true abilities before the Grand Assembly." His gaze swept slowly around the courtyard, meeting one pair of bright, young, burning eyes after another. "This item is the prize — Qiu only hopes the gathered heroes will not find it too modest."

With that, he signaled the servants to lift the red silk cloth and let everyone see.

The servant holding the tray pulled the red silk aside to reveal a robe folded neatly beneath. People were just beginning to wonder, when the other two servants stepped forward, each taking one end, and climbed the stone steps. They shook the robe open — and in that single instant, every person present was moved.

The unfolded robe rippled like a cascading waterfall of black, a flow of dark silk pouring wide, carrying a scattering of snow-white blossoms floating across its surface. Every eye was instantly seized. After a moment, the crowd came back to itself and looked more carefully: it was a black silk outer robe with a lustrous, fluid sheen. At the hem and on the wide sleeves, each bore a border of delicate, snow-white Banyin blossoms, and along every edge of the robe ran a fine thread of gold — making the whole garment at once understated and exquisite, at once grand and shot through with an air of mystery. People stared for a while longer, and then made a discovery that surprised them: the robe was the same on both sides, and the Banyin blossoms on it looked exactly alike whether viewed from front or back. And then they discovered something that truly astonished them: the robe appeared to have no visible seams anywhere. Could it be that it was stitched without a single stitch showing?

"This robe was woven by my daughter from Jade Silkworm silk of Jiulun Mountain." Qiu Changtian's quiet explanation struck every heart in the courtyard like a drum, making each one tremble.

Jiulun Mountain Jade Silkworm silk — that was a treasure of extraordinary rarity. Impervious to water and flame, and more importantly, of extreme suppleness and toughness: short of a divine weapon or artifact, no blade or spear could pierce it. And moreover... that was woven by the hand of Longsky Manor's own Miss Qiu...

"My daughter has named this robe the 'Celestial Silk Robe.' Whoever takes first place today — this shall be their prize."

The moment Qiu Changtian finished speaking, every mind was cleared and sharpened.

First place! That was what mattered most!

And moreover... connecting what Qiu Changtian had said before and after — in that moment, every person present understood exactly what he meant. Hearts that were already eager became impossible to restrain.

chapters.title: Chapter Three: The Grand Gathering at Longsky (Part Two)
chapters.content:
"So that is it — no wonder, no wonder indeed!" Yuwen Luo had seen and heard everything, and could not stop marveling.

"No wonder what?" Ning Lang was still dazzled by the Celestial Silk Robe.

"No wonder so many young and gifted martial artists came — and all of them the most outstanding of their respective families and sects." Yuwen Luo swept his gaze once more over the assembled crowd and sighed again.

Ning Lang blinked, looking at Yuwen Luo with puzzlement. He did not quite understand what the Celestial Silk Robe had to do with all these skilled young fighters.

"You don't understand, do you?" Yuwen Luo glanced sideways at Ning Lang and gave the top of his head a pat. "I wasn't expecting you to."

"Big Brother."

Ning Lang reached up and removed the hand from his head.

"Did you follow what Senior Qiu just said?" Yuwen Luo let the subject of his head drop and continued. "In plain terms, what he was saying was: the Lanyin Biyue — Qiu here is too old and too tired to bother fighting over it. You young people go ahead and scramble for it. But first, have a little warm-up bout at my manor, let me see what you're all made of, and I'll give the standout something nice as a reward."

"Oh — I did know that, Senior Qiu said it himself just now."

"The important part is the reward." Yuwen Luo's brow lifted meaningfully. "This Celestial Silk Robe was woven by the apple of Senior Qiu's eye with her own hands. Do you understand now? What does a young woman weave for? She weaves for her husband! The old man is plainly picking a son-in-law! Not only picking a son-in-law — he's picking a Lanyin Order Master! Today's champion is tomorrow's son-in-law of Longsky Manor and the day after's sovereign of the martial world!"

"Ah?" Ning Lang's eyes went wide. He had thought it was just young people having a friendly spar — how could it hold so many layers of meaning?

"So look at this courtyard," Yuwen Luo swept an arm wide, "is there anyone here who is not a name known throughout the jianghu? Which one of them doesn't dream of becoming the Lanyin Order Master? And if a person could earn the backing of the Qiu family of Longsky Manor, one of the Six Great Clans — why, that would be like already having a finger touching the Lanyin Order. That is no small thing!"

Yuwen Luo's gaze drifted toward the Celestial Silk Robe, a trace of longing in his eyes. "And moreover, the young lady of the Qiu family is known as a beauty throughout the jianghu. 'Autumn river waves, a beauty past compare' — that is not an empty phrase. I too would very much like to marry such a beauty and become the Lanyin Order Master."

"Then Big Brother should just go and compete." Ning Lang offered the suggestion earnestly.

"Hmph!" Yuwen Luo gritted his teeth. "If only I had the martial skill for it!"

"Then..."

"Then what? There's nothing for it but to watch! Watching is all I can do!" Yuwen Luo's head drooped, the air deflating out of him slightly. "Besides, if I dared go up there, my older brother would shatter my skull for it... right, speaking of which — you know I'm from the Yuwen family, don't you?"

"Ah?" Ning Lang was surprised.

Yuwen Luo looked at his face and felt truly hopeless. "The moment I saw that silver spear on your back, I knew you were from the Ning family. We've been traveling together for nearly a month now and you still didn't know I was from the Yuwen family?! And besides..." He pointed toward Yuwen Feng in the small pavilion. "Would someone who can sit beside Qiu Changtian and who happens to be surnamed Yuwen be an ordinary person? Why does that brain of yours never make an extra turn or two?"

"There are plenty of people in the world with the surname Yuwen, and it's not like only someone from the Yuwen great clan can sit beside Senior Qiu." Ning Lang actually said something rather clever this time, leaving Yuwen Luo with nothing to say.

Yuwen Luo looked at him, then nodded slowly. "Under my brilliant guidance, you truly are making progress. Now, let your brother teach you to recognize a few more faces." He pointed toward the small central pavilion. "The white-faced, slightly stout young man sitting beside my older brother, the cheerful-looking one — that is Hua Qinghe, the eldest son of the Hua family of Bai Province. His family also has a younger sister — a beauty on par with the young lady of the Qiu family. 'Flower shadows swaying, heaven-given beauty; autumn river waves, a loveliness past compare' — these two lines describe the two great beauties of the martial world, north and south: Hua Fushu and Qiu Hengbo. I haven't yet seen Qiu Hengbo in person, but Hua Fushu..." Yuwen Luo's eyes narrowed dreamily as if summoning the memory of the Hua family's young mistress to mind. "Flower shadow, swaying, heaven-given grace — quite genuinely so."

"Mm." Ning Lang had little reaction to the beauties Yuwen Luo was rhapsodizing over. He pointed at the small pavilion. "And who's sitting behind Senior Nan?"

Yuwen Luo looked at the man in question and immediately grew serious. "Mei Hongming, the sect's senior disciple at Taoluo Gate. Don't let that fragile-scholar look fool you — he is a formidable figure. I would sooner provoke my older brother than cross anyone from Taoluo Gate."

"Why?"

"'Qianbei sword, Cangyun blade, Fengwu palm, Taoluo hidden weapons' — this saying describes the specialty of each of the Four Great Schools. Taoluo Gate's claim to fame is its hidden weapons. Compared to swords, blades, and bare-hand techniques, hidden weapons are something against which there is almost no defense. And Taoluo Gate's hidden weapons are specifically aimed at the extraordinary meridians and acupoints of the body — a light hit and you lose a portion of your power; a direct hit can cripple your martial arts or take your life. So among the Four Great Schools, the most feared is not the Fengwu School, which has produced five generations of Lanyin Order Masters, but Taoluo Gate, which has always kept quietly to itself. And don't be deceived by the names they give their hidden weapons — the more elegantly they're named, the more deadly they are. 'Spring Night Silk Rain,' 'Summer Day Reflected Lotus,' 'Autumn Wind White Dew,' 'Winter Plum Blossoms in Snow' — the prettier the name, the more vicious the sting."

"I see." Ning Lang made a note of it.

"That woman in Daoist robes with the handsome face and the cold expression is the senior disciple of Nanling Feixue Abbey, Shang Pinghan. That large, thick-bearded man is Wei Lang, head of the Black Cloud Stronghold. That man in the red robe with the whisk is Jin Quelou of the 'Three Thousand Buddha Palms'..."

While Yuwen Luo was busy introducing the jianghu figures, on the other side Qiu Changtian was explaining the rules of the bout.

"This gathering is purely a meeting of friends through martial arts, so Qiu has not set up a formal arena. The open space of two zhang directly in front of this pavilion will serve as our ring. When you compete, please show restraint — stop when the point is made and do not let it damage our friendship. Furthermore, I ask that you refrain from harming the flowers and furnishings of this courtyard — they are the work of my daughter's own hands."

Some felt a little dissatisfied at these words, yet thinking of Qiu Changtian's name as a benevolent hero, such a request was entirely in keeping with his character. And looking around this elegantly arranged courtyard, knowing it had all been done by the Qiu young mistress's hand, those restless hearts smoothed themselves over.

"Bouts may be literary or martial, as each person sees fit. And now Qiu will speak no further — whoever among the heroes wishes to go first, please step forward."

The moment Qiu Changtian finished, many people very much wanted to be that "first person" — and yet, every gaze instinctively moved toward the small pavilion. Eyes weighed and measured and deliberated, and in the end, still hesitated. The courtyard sank into a thick, frozen silence.

After a long pause, someone finally broke that silence, stepped forward, clasped their hands, and asked with barely concealed hope: "Dare I ask whether the Seventh Young Master and the Second Young Master intend to participate?"

This was the question many had in their hearts, and at last someone had put it to voice. The entire courtyard turned with relief and gratitude toward that person, then fixed every gaze with barely concealed hope on the pavilion's two occupants. Even if their reputations exceeded their actual skill, still — if these two did not take part, so much the better!

Qiu Changtian and Nan Wofeng turned toward Lan Qi and Ming Er with composed smiles.

"Ha..." Lan Qi's jade fan turned with an easy flick, and those jade-green eyes made a slow circuit of the courtyard. Every person present felt something tugging at their soul, a slight involuntary sway. "Today's gathering is truly rare, and to meet the Second Young Master of the Ming family here — how could I pass that up?"

Those words landed lightly, effortlessly enthralling — the assembled heroes floated for just a moment, and then understood.

Of course I am entering, but as for all of you — I see none of you. The only opponent worth my notice is Ming Er.

A moment of silence in the courtyard, followed by a wave of cold snorts, the sharpest of which came from the small pavilion itself.

"Rather, it is I who should seize this rare opportunity to seek guidance from the gathered heroes and from the Seventh Young Master." Ming Er rose to his feet with clasped hands, his manner easy and graceful, his gaze sweeping the assembled heroes once before settling into a faint smile that made everyone who saw it feel at ease.

So right — a demon is simply no match for an immortal! The assembled heroes let out a collective breath of relief.

A cold, haughty figure walked out of the small pavilion.

"Yuwen Feng, in his mediocrity, will be the first — to seek the guidance of the gathered heroes." Yuwen Feng clasped his hands, swept his gaze around the courtyard, and then allowed it to land on Lan Qi — where it stayed, rooted, unmoving.

The courtyard held its breath. Yuwen's eldest son, facing off against the Lan family's seventh young master — who would win?

"Ha ha..." Lan Qi laughed freely, jade fan swaying, shoulder ribbons drifting, wind-borne elegance and wicked charm filling the courtyard, "What a day — what a day indeed! To witness the great Yuwen eldest son face the heroes of all the world with his bare hands — truly an achievement unmatched in all of history! What extraordinary fortune I have, to behold such a sight with my own eyes!"

At those words, Yuwen Feng's eyes, always carrying their air of arrogance, cooled by several degrees. And in the courtyard, after a moment of blank disbelief, there was a surge of barely suppressed delight — and a few people who had until recently been cursing the "jade demon" now actually felt a flicker of gratitude toward him.

"Big Brother is in real trouble this time." Watching from a distance, Yuwen Luo could only shake his head.

"Why?" Ning Lang was puzzled.

"Big Brother originally stepped out to challenge Lan Qi directly — but with a single offhand remark, Lan Qi deflected it, and now my big brother has no choice but to fight bare-handed against the entire courtyard, one after another, until he beats every opponent or is beaten himself." Yuwen Luo looked worried.

"But Senior Qiu didn't say weapons were forbidden — and your big brother doesn't have to listen to whatever Lan... the Seventh Young Master says." Ning Lang pointed out.

"My big brother is too proud to hand anyone that opening." Yuwen Luo glanced sideways at him, then shifted his gaze back to Lan Qi, who was making an elegant show of fanning himself inside the pavilion. "They really didn't give him that name 'jade demon' for nothing."

Ning Lang heard this, pressed his lips together, and opened his mouth to say something — then, in the end, closed it again.

Yuwen Feng shot a final furious look at Lan Qi, then turned away with his head high. "Then Yuwen Feng will take on the gathered heroes with these two bare palms of his."

Qiu Changtian and Nan Wofeng exchanged a glance at those words, each frowning slightly — but neither said anything.

The assembled heroes in the courtyard heard this and felt a mixture of indignation and suppressed glee.

You are Yuwen Feng, eldest son of the Yuwen family — granted. You are young and already renowned for your skill — granted. Your Scarlet Dragon Whip has swept the jianghu with few opponents — granted. But to announce openly that you will fight the heroes of all the world bare-handed is simply too arrogant. Even Lan Qi, for all his swagger, at least acknowledged there was an opponent worth facing — and did not proclaim himself unrivaled under heaven!

But after the indignation came the unavoidable private delight.

The Yuwen family's Scarlet Dragon Whip was not something to trifle with, and this Yuwen Feng even less so — arrogant, haughty, contemptuous of all others. The moment he entered the jianghu, he had offended any number of people, yet his martial skill was undeniably real. Countless seasoned veterans had been swept off their feet by that whip of his — dignity and reputation both shattered in one stroke. But now he had the nerve to pit two bare hands against the whole courtyard... hmph. Old grudges and fresh wrongs — if not now, then when?

"Jin Quelou presumes to seek the Yuwen young master's instruction."

While the rest of the courtyard was still weighing whether to be the first to challenge Yuwen Feng — full of energy, at ten full parts of his power — a clear, confident voice rang out, and a tall man in red rose from his seat, whisk in hand, and walked toward Yuwen Feng.

"Ah, it is the 'Three Thousand Buddha Palms' young hero Jin." Yuwen Feng raised an eye to look at his first opponent.

"Indeed." Jin Quelou's whisk lifted in a graceful arc. "I ask the Yuwen young master to show mercy."

"We each do our best — what point is there in such pleasantries?" Yuwen Feng answered with a cold laugh.

"Please." Jin Quelou settled his stance with composure.

"Let me first see whether the Three Thousand Buddha Palms really holds three thousand variations."

Still speaking, Yuwen Feng extended his left palm, reaching toward the whisk bundled against Jin Quelou's arm. The gesture looked almost careless and unhurried, but halfway there that palm became swift as a rushing wind. In the blink of an eye it had reached Jin Quelou, the whisk nearly between those fingers — and then a flash of red as Jin Quelou's foot pivoted to the side and the whole body slid one foot sideways, just barely clearing the reach.

A collective held breath — a few people silently cried "well done!" A few others broke into a cold sweat, thinking: had that been me, I might not have gotten clear.

"Young hero Jin's whisk is clearly not something to be seen by just anyone."

The words came out lightly, but the hand did not pause. That extended left palm shifted shape and cut sideways, slicing toward the cascade of whisk threads hanging at Jin Quelou's wrist. That single palm carried the rumble of wind and thunder within its lightness. Jin Quelou dared not be slow — with a flick of the hand the whisk lifted, and three thousand threads transformed into silken ribbons spinning to envelop that cutting palm. Yuwen Feng neither dodged nor retreated but turned his palm over, opening it to meet the incoming threads — and the gesture looked as though the whisk were delivering itself into his hand. Jin Quelou saw it and inwardly cried disaster, but his face did not change. In an instant his wrist turned, inner force surged through his palm, and the threads burst apart, each one shooting toward Yuwen Feng's open left hand like steel needles. They were barely an inch from the palm now — if they hit, that hand would surely be destroyed.

"Ah!" Someone could not hold back a cry of alarm.

"Hmph!" Yuwen Feng's cold snort rang out, and the watching crowd witnessed what looked like a miracle — a sleeve slid down at precisely the right moment and caught every last thread. Before anyone could hail the move, the sleeve rolled inward and the threads were gone. The sleeve flicked open, metal rang out twice, and when it separated from the whisk, both figures stepped back one pace each.

They regarded each other for a moment. Then Jin Quelou clasped his hands. "I concede." He turned and walked back to his seat.

The crowd, hearing this, was genuinely surprised. The two had exchanged only a few moves — each one a blur of change and shift, and with only one hand apiece, the bout had already been extraordinary. They had all been holding their breath in total concentration, and were just preparing to watch it build further — and then someone had conceded. Clearly no decisive outcome had yet been reached.

chapters.title: Chapter Three: The Grand Gathering at Longsky (Part Three)
chapters.content:
In the small central pavilion, Lan Qi smiled faintly, opened his jade fan, and raised it to half-conceal his face, leaving only those jade-green eyes afloat above the rim, amusement rippling in their depths.

Ming Er's expression remained unchanged, his misty eyes resting on Yuwen Feng with quiet attention.

Qiu Changtian and Nan Wofeng smiled and nodded with the composure of men who had seen and understood.

"Big Brother, your older brother is undeniably skilled — but that Jin hero is the more admirable man of the two." Ning Lang looked at the barely visible inch of silver whisk thread caught beneath Yuwen Feng's foot and said so, then turned with genuine respect toward Jin Quelou, who had returned to his seat with perfect calm.

"Mm." Yuwen Luo, still writing, gave a firm nod. "The jianghu says he is devoted to Shang Pinghan of Feixue Abbey. That move was likely on her account — my older brother once wrapped his whip around Shang Pinghan's sword and twisted it into nine pieces."

"Oh?" Ning Lang turned back to look at Yuwen Luo. "Why would he be fond of a Daoist nun? Daoists are people set apart from the mortal world."

"There are monks who fall for Buddhist nuns!" Yuwen Luo rolled his eyes and lifted his brush to point at Ning Lang's chest. "Caring for someone comes from here." The brush tip then moved to tap his head. "This part cannot control it. Who knows — someday you might find yourself falling for someone even more improbable."

"Ah... I wouldn't care for just anyone." Ning Lang's face reddened faintly, and he said something a little dazed.

"If not just anyone, then who would you care for?" Yuwen Luo snorted dismissively and bent his head back to his great work.

"A man ought to care for his wife." Ning Lang answered quite seriously.

Yuwen Luo actually looked up at that, regarded Ning Lang for a moment, and then bent back over his writing. "Many men loathe that idea."

"Wei Lang seeks the Yuwen young master's guidance."

Ning Lang was about to say more when the Black Cloud Stronghold's head approached Yuwen Feng, and his attention was immediately caught. He said no more.

While everyone else was focused on the contest, someone at the edge of the gate had turned and was walking away, deeper into the grounds of Longsky Manor.

At the very deepest point of the manor, a sheer natural cliff face rose high and imposing.

Rounding the cliff, the space opened suddenly into a wide, sweeping hillside. At its far end stood the sheer vertical walls of Tianzhi Mountain, forming with the cliff behind it a natural barrier that sealed off the world beyond.

The hillside was thick with Banyin blossoms — layer on layer, high and low, near and far, their white as flawless as moonlight — swaying in the mountain breeze in a sea of snow and silver. Beneath a blue sky and green mountains, this place was like a landscape from a dream.

In the midst of that sea of snow and moon, an embroidery frame was stretched out on a slope. A young woman in a pale blue skirt sat before it, head bowed in concentration, working with both hands at once — a sight that made every onlooker blink in astonishment. Her slender hands flew, needles threading and weaving without pause, and on the cloth, grass and earth, hillside and cliff, Banyin blossoms and wild birds and insects came to life one by one — the flowers vivid, the birds seemingly ready to take wing, the cliff face like a painting. Her needlework was matchless, her stitching like something divine.

A small yellow butterfly flitted through the sea of blossoms — right, then left, then up, then down — and at last settled lightly on a painted flower's heart within the embroidery. The young woman's wrist shifted; a silver needle flew. And now that yellow butterfly was forever dancing in this dream-garden of illusion.

"Miss."

A girl as slender as a new willow had slipped in from behind the cliff face, moving so lightly her steps made no sound. This single soft call was refined to the very limit of softness.

The silver needle was set aside, the colored thread knotted off, and on the embroidery cloth, a world of flowers unreachable by any dust of the mortal realm was now complete.

A fingertip moved; the silver needle disappeared into her sleeve. The young woman raised her head — and in that instant, one felt that every rise and fall of those snow-white blossoms was a bow of reverence to her.

"Liumo, how are things up front?" The young woman's voice flowed like light ripples over still water.

"Miss, it is not only that the famous heroes from every direction have arrived — even the Second Young Master of the Ming family and the Seventh Young Master of the Lan family are here." The excitement and delight in Liumo's voice was impossible to contain. "At this moment, the eldest son of the Yuwen family is fighting the head of the Black Cloud Stronghold bare-handed, having already defeated Jin Quelou of the 'Three Thousand Buddha Palms.'"

"Oh?" The young woman's willow-leaf brows arched faintly upward.

"I had a good look just now. Among all those young martial artists, a number of them have fine figures and handsome looks. But in terms of bearing and family standing, the young masters of the great families are naturally the finest — except for the eldest Hua son being a little stout, all the others are young and good-looking. And the two most remarkable by far are the Second Young Master and the Seventh Young Master." When she came to those two, Liumo's eyes lit up. "They look... they look so... so handsome I can't think how to say it. Looking at the Second Young Master I think of immortals; looking at the Seventh Young Master I feel my very soul no longer belongs to me."

"Ha..." The young woman in the pale blue skirt couldn't help but smile faintly at this description, a soft warmth flowing through her almond eyes, a quality of rare, poised beauty. "Then both must be as the rumors describe them. And yet..."

"And yet what?" Liumo asked.

"Did Lie Chifeng not come?" The young woman answered with another question instead.

"He did not." Liumo answered, and then her eyes darted sideways. "Then could it be that the one Miss favors is..."

Before Liumo could finish, the young woman raised a hand to stop the second half of that sentence. "These three are the most distinguished and extraordinary of the younger generation in the martial world today. Only..." She paused softly before adding, in a very low voice: "Men of that kind are not suited to be a husband."

"Ah? But why?" Liumo was bewildered. What woman in the world would not dream of marrying such a man?

The young woman smiled and shook her head without answering. "You said just now that Yuwen Feng was fighting bare-handed — how did that come about? The Yuwen family is known throughout the jianghu for the Scarlet Dragon Whip."

"Oh, that..." Liumo recounted everything she had seen and heard in the courtyard from beginning to end.

"I see." The young woman nodded inwardly, and something like a quiet, slight sigh entered her voice. "Young Yuwen Feng has made a name for himself early — a truly impressive figure. But he is too rigid and too proud. Something so unyielding will snap."

"Miss, those people..." Liumo looked at her, then asked in a soft voice: "Who does Miss hope will receive the Celestial Silk Robe?"

"That... Father will surely choose the finest person." The young woman said gently.

"The finest?" Liumo thought it over. "That would be the Second Young Master or the Seventh Young Master, I should think." She tilted her head to look at her young mistress, whose beauty had no equal, and felt a warmth of gladness on her behalf. "Both are accomplished in every way. Either would be a perfect match for Miss — an absolute pairing made in heaven."

"Ming Er and Lan Qi?" The young woman raised her eyes toward the hillside covered in Banyin blossoms.

Back in the courtyard, the round of bouts came to an end: Yuwen Feng defeated Wei Lang.

Wei Lang had barely stepped down when another challenger stepped forward.

"Big Brother, is your older brother truly going to keep fighting all these people by himself?" Ning Lang watched Yuwen Feng and felt a little worried.

That last exchange had been entirely different from the one before it — the Black Cloud Stronghold head fought with brute, solid power, every move landing with full weight. Yuwen Feng had looked at ease as he answered each one and ultimately won, but the few drops of sweat that had appeared at his temple told another story. He had spent real energy. And there were still so many others in the courtyard — could he truly hold out to the end with bare hands? Worse still, there were those two whose depths were completely unreadable — Ming Er and Lan Qi.

"That is the kind of person he is. He would rather be broken than show weakness." Yuwen Luo gripped the brush in his hand, still writing.

"Is there truly nothing to be done?" Ning Lang's worry showed.

The next bout had already begun. This opponent's skill was actually no lower than Wei Lang's or Jin Quelou's, and his footwork was exceptionally agile. In a space of two zhang, he leapt and dodged as though he had a field of two hundred to move in — darting left and right, soaring up and dropping down — making anyone who watched dizzy and exhausted, to say nothing of his opponent.

"There is one thing that could be done." Yuwen Luo set down his brush, gaze moving to the small central pavilion. "If someone with higher skill than my brother went up and defeated him — but..." He paused.

"But what?" Ning Lang pressed.

"The two people in this garden who can surpass him won't step in." Yuwen Luo swept his eyes across the courtyard and brought them to rest again on the pavilion. "And the other two — about equal to my brother in skill. If they fought, knowing my older brother's temperament, it would likely go to the very edge of life and death before either conceded. Going up would only make things worse."

"Then..."

"Watch and see." Yuwen Luo shifted his gaze back to the bout.

With a sharp cry from Yuwen Feng, a figure flew and landed hard — the bout was over. Yuwen Feng had won again.

The defeated man had barely stepped back when another came forward — and this time not empty-handed. A great broadsword rested on his shoulder, his frame broad and imposing as a small hill, brows thick and fierce as temple guardians, utterly formidable.

"This is bad." One look at the new challenger and Yuwen Luo gave a helpless laugh.

"Is it bad? Is this person very skilled?" Ning Lang asked quickly.

"Not in that way." Yuwen Luo shook his head. "Zhou Da of the 'Ghost-Head Blade' is a skilled fighter, but his martial skill falls well short of my older brother's. The problem is his natural strength — that blade alone weighs a hundred and twenty catties. Add his arm strength on top of that... ah, even if my older brother wins, he'll likely burn through sixty percent of his remaining power just doing it."

Before Yuwen Luo had finished, the two had already begun. Yuwen Feng continued with bare hands, while Zhou Da swung his blade like a man gone mad — every chop sending a gust of wind through the courtyard strong enough to make the Banyin blossoms sway and tremble. The ones closest to the fighting either snapped at the stem and fell to the ground or were sent flying, pot and all. Qiu Changtian watched and drew his brows together sharply.

"That name 'Ghost-Head Blade' was misapplied, wasn't it?" Lan Qi was heard to murmur. "It ought to be 'Madman's Blade' — a man who can lay ruin to flowers like this..."

The words were barely above a whisper, yet in the stillness of the courtyard, every person — including the two men locked in combat — heard them clearly.

"Ha!" A great bellow from Zhou Da, and his broadsword came crashing down with redoubled ferocity. In an instant a fierce wind rose, and several pots of Banyin were lifted and sent spinning into the air.

"Ah, what a shame — to treat something born of a woman's hands so carelessly."

A soft murmur — and then Lan Qi rose from his seat with unhurried ease, stepped down from the small pavilion with unhurried ease, and walked in a perfectly straight line — completely unhurried — toward the two men in the midst of their fight. Yuwen Feng's palm, Zhou Da's blade: as each was about to land on him, each paused — as though something had blocked them — just for an instant. Then the palm fell, the blade came down, Yuwen Feng's palm caught the blade's handle and Zhou Da's handle caught Yuwen Feng's palm — and Lan Qi had already walked through the space between them and out the other side.

His movements appeared slow, yet by the time he had passed, those airborne pots of flowers had not yet fallen to earth. He raised a hand — one pot landed in his palm. He moved his hand — the pot floated gently back to its place. He raised his hand again, moved it again, and one by one every pot that had been sent spinning into the air descended back to its rightful place. Then he bent down and began picking up, one by one, the Banyin stems that had been snapped off and fallen to the ground by the wind of the blade.

The bout continued around him; blasts of palm force and sword wind swept his robes — but left him untouched. Cradling the broken blossoms, he made his unhurried way back to the small pavilion, settled into his seat, and sat there entirely unharmed.

"Boom!"

The sound of the broadsword striking the stone floor rang out.

Zhou Da knelt awkwardly on the ground, both hands still gripping the blade's handle. A foot was resting on the blade's spine. Following that foot upward: Yuwen Feng, looking down at him from above.

"If you would be so kind — put these flowers in water."

The whole courtyard was watching the outcome of the bout, but Lan Qi gave it no notice whatsoever. He simply extended the blossoms in his arms toward Qiu Zang, who stood beside the pavilion.

Caught in those jade-green eyes for one unguarded moment, Qiu Zang stepped forward without thinking and accepted the flowers.

chapters.title: Chapter Four: Born Rivals (Part One)
chapters.content:
"Yuwen Feng seeks the guidance of the Seventh Young Master!"

The voice rang out, proud and edged with anger. Yuwen Feng pointed directly at Lan Qi, dismissing entirely the challenger who had already walked halfway toward him, dismissing entirely the stunned eyes of every person in the courtyard, his gaze fixed and unblinking on the man sitting in the pavilion with his easy, insolent smile.

Lan Qi's eyes turned toward Yuwen Feng. He raised one brow. He did not move. A slow swing of the jade fan — and a smile of unfathomable meaning settled on his face.

"Yuwen Feng seeks the guidance of the Seventh Young Master!" The same words, the same resolute voice, as Yuwen Feng's gaze drilled into Lan Qi and refused to let go.

Lan Qi rose, every movement unhurried and elegant. The smile on his face remained. And as he stepped down from the pavilion, the challenger who had been standing halfway to Yuwen Feng felt a chill run suddenly up his spine, and found his feet stepping backward of their own accord, one by one, until he was back in his original seat.

Yuwen Feng stood perfectly straight and cold, watching his opponent approach.

"Qiu considers himself a man of little talent, and yet the great eldest son of the Yuwen family has singled me out by name — what an honor." Lan Qi sauntered with leisure to a stop before Yuwen Feng. "Such warm regard from the young master — how could I not offer something in return?" The trailing note of the last syllable was drawn out just slightly, like an invisible thread of silk coiling around the ear and drawing the listener's whole attention toward it.

"The young master has already fought four rounds and must be fatigued. It would be ungentlemanly for me to take advantage of that. In the spirit of fairness..." Lan Qi's jade fan lifted to cover his lips, leaving only those jade-green eyes afloat — waves of light rippling within them, flowing like a river of cool spring water on a blazing summer day, spilling a dazed enchantment through the entire courtyard. Even Yuwen Feng, who was full of burning fury, was lost for just one instant.

Demon.

That single word rose silently in the hearts of many people present — Yuwen Feng included.

"I shall face you with one finger, in tribute to the respect I hold for the young master."

The words entered, somehow, in a half-dream — yet clear as a bell, letter by letter. In an instant every pair of eyes in the courtyard went wide, fixed on the man who had said this with such an easy smile, as though no one could quite trust what they had just heard.

"You..." The rage surged and broke in a single breath — Yuwen Feng's entire body trembled, his eyes blazing crimson, his teeth clenched around the words he stared through at Lan Qi.

The jade fan folded slowly shut to reveal red lips and white teeth, which parted — slowly, lightly — to breathe out: "Surely the young master does not find this unfair?" One long, slender forefinger moved in a gentle wag, and the jade-green eyes narrowed just slightly. To everyone else it looked like nothing but bewitching elegance — but Yuwen Feng saw it with perfect clarity: the glint of arrogance and contempt seeping from the corner of those eyes. "Or, if I am not even permitted a single finger — should I perhaps be limited to my feet?" The jade-green eyes dropped, just barely, letting their gaze drift downward.

In that moment, Yuwen Feng felt as though those eyes had settled on him — looking down at him with that cool, unmistakable disdain, as one might regard the dust beneath one's feet. A roar went through his blood, through every inch of his body.

"No!" His teeth ground together until they nearly bled. "Every person in the martial world knows the Seventh Young Master's skill is unmatched. For Yuwen Feng to have even one finger of yours raised against him would already be the highest honor — I can only be grateful. How could there be any other thought?"

"Oh, young master is too modest." The jade fan swung open; Lan Qi smiled with the deepest contentment.

Going too far. Yuwen Feng's fists clenched so hard his knuckles cracked.

"Then I ask the Seventh Young Master's instruction!"
